The "Great Plan" is a text that elucidates the Way, and therefore it investigates the nexus between Heaven and humankind with the utmost precision; the Spring and Autumn Annals is a record of events, so it could only record the calamities and anomalies themselves. Sometimes Heaven sends down a calamity first and human affairs respond afterward; sometimes human affairs go awry first and Heaven sends down a calamity afterward—at the nearest within ten days or a month, and at the farthest across several decades. Since the Sage tied events to specific days and months, how could he string them together in his writing? Once one connects the phrasing and pairs the events, to insist on stating, "Such-and-such an affair caused such-and-such a calamity; such-and-such a calamity responded to such-and-such an affair"—how could that be the style of the Spring and Autumn Annals? Therefore, the affairs of the Spring and Autumn Annals are all brought out in the commentaries; it is not merely that it leaves the correspondences of calamities unrecorded. The correspondences of human affairs in the "Great Plan" were explicitly stated by Jizi 箕子, and were moreover not the wild fabrications of Han-dynasty Confucians. Their method is set forth in outline in the histories of the two Han dynasties. Ban Gu 班固, basing himself on the ideas of Liu Xiang 劉向, composed the "Treatise on the Five Phases" (Wuxing zhi) in five chapters (juan); Fan Ye 范曄, following Ban Gu's precedent, composed the "Treatise on the Five Phases" in six chapters, which had been completed by Sima Biao 司馬彪. All of them tied the disturbances of the Five Phases to the Five Affairs, and matched the correspondences of the Five Affairs to the Five Phases, drawing eclectically upon the Zuo Commentary (Zuozhuan), the Discourses of the States (Guoyu), the Book of Lineages (Shiben), and recent events of the two Han dynasties to elucidate the "Various Verifications" (shuzheng), ultimately tracing them back to the ruler's…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
主一心起處動止靡不有應蘇軾以歆向
父子所言互異又以八政五紀强附于庶
徵謂其牽合而譏之未嘗盡以爲非也夫
二子之學雜而不貫則誠有之乃一代所
崇重與春秋洪範之遺法往往而在夫安
得而盡廢之如稱田獵不宿飲食不饗之
屬致木不曲直而貌之不恭厥極惡時則
金沴木好攻戰飾城郭之屬致金不從革
而言之不從厥極憂時則木沴金棄法律
===
逐功臣之屬致火不炎上而視之不明厥
極疾時則水沴火簡宗廟廢祭祀之屬致
水不潤下而聽之不聰厥極貧時則火沴
水治宮室犯親戚之屬致稼穡不成而思
之不睿厥極凶時則金木水火沴土極之
不建厥咎眊厥罰恒陰厥極弱時則有日
月星辰孛薄之異其說如此人惟視五行
爲虛位爕理爲空言于是曲學者有堯湯
水旱之對尚通者有行期適會之言而訣
punctuated: 主一心，起處動止，靡不有應。蘇軾以歆、向父子所言互異，又以八政、五紀强附于庶徵，謂其牽合而譏之，未嘗盡以爲非也。夫二子之學，雜而不貫，則誠有之；乃一代所崇重，與《春秋》、《洪範》之遺法往往而在，夫安得而盡廢之？如稱田獵不宿、飲食不饗之屬，致木不曲直；而貌之不恭，厥極惡，時則金沴木。好攻戰、飾城郭之屬，致金不從革；而言之不從，厥極憂，時則木沴金。棄法律、逐功臣之屬，致火不炎上；而視之不明，厥極疾，時則水沴火。簡宗廟、廢祭祀之屬，致水不潤下；而聽之不聰，厥極貧，時則火沴水。治宮室、犯親戚之屬，致稼穡不成；而思之不睿，厥極凶，時則金木水火沴土。極之不建，厥咎眊，厥罰恒陰，厥極弱，時則有日月星辰孛薄之異。其說如此。人惟視五行爲虛位、爕理爲空言，于是曲學者有堯、湯水旱之對，尚通者有行期適會之言，而訣端見矣。
translation_en: … the ruler's single mind, so that in his rising and resting, his movement and stillness, there is nothing to which nature does not respond. Because the explanations given by the father and son Liu Xiang 劉向 and Liu Xin 劉歆 differed from one another, and because they forcibly attached the Eight Objects of Government (bazheng 八政) and the Five Arrangements of Time (wuji 五紀) to the Various Verifications (shuzheng 庶徵), Su Shi 蘇軾 criticized their theories as strained; yet he never dismissed them as entirely wrong. That the learning of the two masters was miscellaneous and lacked unity is indeed true; nevertheless, what was revered by a whole dynasty, along with the surviving methods of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu 春秋) and the "Great Plan" (Hongfan 洪範), are often preserved therein—how, then, could one discard them completely? For example, they stated that acts such as hunting out of season and holding banquets without proper ritual cause wood not to bend and straighten; and when demeanor is not respectful, the extreme result is ugliness, at which time metal encroaches upon wood. Delighting in offensive warfare, embellishing city walls, and the like cause metal not to obey and change; and when speech is not followed, the extreme result is sorrow, at which time wood encroaches upon metal. Abandoning laws and statutes, expelling meritorious ministers, and the like cause fire not to flare upward; and when sight is not clear, the extreme result is sickness, at which time water encroaches upon fire. Neglecting the ancestral temples, abolishing sacrifices, and the like cause water not to soak and descend; and when hearing is not acute, the extreme result is poverty, at which time fire encroaches upon water.Lavishly building palaces, offending against imperial relatives, and the like cause sowing and reaping not to come to fruition; and when thought is not perspicacious, the extreme result is shortening of life, at which time metal, wood, water, and fire encroach upon earth. When the Royal Perfection (huangji 皇極) is not established, the fault is dimness of spirit, the punishment is constant overcast skies, and the extreme result is weakness, at which time there occur the anomalies of eclipses and comets among the sun, moon, and stars. Such were their doctrines. Only when men came to regard the Five Phases as empty placeholders and the harmonizing of yin and yang as hollow words did sycophantic scholars offer replies citing the floods of Yao 堯 and the droughts of Tang 湯, and those who prized expediency speak of celestial movements and fixed cycles merely happening to coincide—and thus heterodox [? 訣, for 詖] beginnings appeared. …

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
端見矣夫當盛漢君臣之際不然也文帝
日食之詔務省繇費以便民水旱疾疫命
列侯議可佐百姓者宣帝以地震博問經
學士律令有可蠲除者上之光武自以適
見日月令有司修職遵度章帝以方春生
養詔罪非殊死且勿案驗當是時人主祇
慎天戒責躬思咎曷嘗不兢兢五行之應
乎陳平言相職當輔人主理陰陽順四時
丙吉不問道傍死人乃問牛喘魏相條奏
===
明堂月令請立四時之官各舉其事調法
天順時爲安宗廟之大禮鮑昱葘告之對
以一人吁嗟王政爲虧丁鴻請改正匡失
以塞天意楊震以地震戊辰日厥位在中
爲近倖持權之象當是時大臣寅恭賛化
省愆進善曷嘗不兢兢五行之應乎時之
學士大夫守其師說精析玄微則董仲舒
劉向爲之冠舒治公羊春秋始推洪範爲
儒者宗其言曰天心仁愛出災害以譴告
punctuated: 端見矣。夫當盛漢君臣之際，不然也。文帝日食之詔，務省繇費以便民；水旱疾疫，命列侯議可佐百姓者。宣帝以地震，博問經學士，律令有可蠲除者上之。光武自以適見日月，令有司修職遵度。章帝以方春生養，詔罪非殊死，且勿案驗。當是時，人主祇慎天戒，責躬思咎，曷嘗不兢兢五行之應乎？陳平言相職當輔人主，理陰陽，順四時。丙吉不問道傍死人，乃問牛喘。魏相條奏《明堂月令》，請立四時之官，各舉其事，調法天順時爲安宗廟之大禮。鮑昱葘告之對，以一人吁嗟，王政爲虧。丁鴻請改正匡失，以塞天意。楊震以地震戊辰日，厥位在中，爲近倖持權之象。當是時，大臣寅恭賛化，省愆進善，曷嘗不兢兢五行之應乎？時之學士大夫，守其師說，精析玄微，則董仲舒、劉向爲之冠。舒治《公羊春秋》，始推《洪範》，爲儒者宗，其言曰：「天心仁愛，出災害以譴告
translation_en:
… [deceitful] beginnings appeared. Yet during the flourishing Han dynasty, the relationship between ruler and minister was not like this. In Emperor Wen's edict on a solar eclipse, he sought to reduce corvée and expenses to convenience the people; during floods, droughts, and epidemics, he ordered the Marquises to deliberate on ways to assist the common people. Because of an earthquake, Emperor Xuan broadly questioned scholars of the Classics, asking them to submit any statutes and ordinances that could be remitted or abolished. Emperor Guangwu, considering that warnings had appeared in the sun and moon, ordered the authorities to attend to their duties and observe the regulations. Because spring was just bringing forth and nurturing life, Emperor Zhang decreed that crimes not punishable by death should for the time being not be investigated or tried. At that time, the rulers reverently heeded the warnings of Heaven, blaming themselves and reflecting on their faults—when were they not cautiously attentive to the responses of the Five Phases?

Chen Ping 陳平 said that the office of Counselor-in-Chief ought to assist the ruler in regulating yin and yang and conforming to the four seasons. Bing Ji 丙吉 did not ask about the dead men by the roadside, but instead asked about a panting ox. Wei Xiang 魏相 submitted an itemized memorial on the Monthly Ordinances of the Bright Hall (Mingtang yueling), requesting the establishment of officials for the four seasons, each to carry out his duties, holding [?] that emulating Heaven and conforming to the seasons was the great ritual for securing the ancestral temple. In his reply concerning warnings of calamities, Bao Yu 鮑昱 held that if a single person sighed in distress, kingly governance was thereby deficient. Ding Hong 丁鴻 requested the correction of errors and rectification of failings in order to satisfy the will of Heaven. Because an earthquake occurred on a wuchen day, whose position is in the center, Yang Zhen 楊震 took it as a portent of close favorites holding power. At that time, the great ministers reverently assisted in the transformative governance, examining faults and advancing goodness—when were they not cautiously attentive to the responses of the Five Phases?

Among the scholars and grandees of the time who upheld their masters' doctrines and finely analyzed the abstruse and subtle, Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒 and Liu Xiang 劉向 stood at the head. Dong Zhongshu studied the Gongyang Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals (Gongyang Chunqiu) and was the first to deduce principles from the "Great Plan" (Hongfan), becoming the patriarch of Confucian scholars. His words were: "The mind of Heaven is benevolent and loving; it sends forth calamities and harm to reprimand and warn …"

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之又出怪異以儆懼之向治穀梁春秋著
五行傳論其言曰和氣致祥乖氣致異祥
多者國安異衆者國危要以究極天人感
動人主二子博極羣書爲漢儒宗皆學春
秋言春秋中災異烏得以其言災異也而
遽剽剝之他若涌水爲災京房懼極陰生
陽翼奉憂寒陰過節郎顗諫東萊黑龍谷
永疏三朝日食孔光徵風雷數發蔡邕對
論者不詳擇其言猥以圖讖術數之流皮
===
傳而弁髦之亦過甚已哉故嘗謂漢近古
有洪範春秋之緒學上自詔制下而疏議
皆有以識達天人知災祲所自來君臣咨
咨動色以爲戒所謂處巖廓之上而慮四
方視千古之前而鏡當代蓋不出戶知天
道猶有此學在焉易曰天垂象見吉凶聖
人象之又曰觀乎天文以察時變故夫三
才之道未易言也其神理乘虛而相通靈
氣旋轉而相薄人居天地之中如龍在天
punctuated: 之，又出怪異以儆懼之。」向治《穀梁春秋》，著《五行傳論》，其言曰：「和氣致祥，乖氣致異；祥多者國安，異衆者國危。」要以究極天人，感動人主。二子博極羣書，爲漢儒宗，皆學《春秋》，言《春秋》中災異。烏得以其言災異也，而遽剽剝之？他若涌水爲災，京房懼極陰生陽；翼奉憂寒陰過節；郎顗諫東萊黑龍；谷永疏三朝日食；孔光徵風雷數發；蔡邕對……論者不詳擇其言，猥以圖讖術數之流，皮傳而弁髦之，亦過甚已哉！故嘗謂漢近古，有《洪範》、《春秋》之緒學，上自詔制，下而疏議，皆有以識達天人，知災祲所自來，君臣咨咨，動色以爲戒。所謂「處巖廓之上而慮四方，視千古之前而鏡當代，蓋不出戶知天道」，猶有此學在焉。《易》曰：「天垂象，見吉凶，聖人象之。」又曰：「觀乎天文，以察時變。」故夫三才之道，未易言也。其神理乘虛而相通，靈氣旋轉而相薄。人居天地之中，如龍在天，
translation_en:
… him, and further sends forth strange anomalies to alarm and frighten him." Liu Xiang 劉向 specialized in the Guliang Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals (Guliang Chunqiu) and authored the Discourse on the Commentary on the Five Phases (Wuxing zhuan lun), in which he said: "Harmonious qi brings about auspicious signs; discordant qi brings about anomalies. When auspicious signs are many, the state is secure; when anomalies are numerous, the state is in peril." In essence, both sought to thoroughly investigate the relationship between Heaven and humanity so as to move the ruler's heart. These two masters were extraordinarily well-read in all books and stood as the patriarchs of Han Confucianism; both studied the Spring and Autumn Annals and discussed the disasters and anomalies recorded within the Spring and Autumn Annals. How could one summarily attack and tear them down merely because they spoke of disasters and anomalies?

As for others—such as Jing Fang 京房, when gushing waters caused disaster, fearing that extreme yin would give rise to yang; Yi Feng 翼奉 worrying over cold and阴 (yin) exceeding their seasonal bounds; Lang Yi 郎顗 remonstrating about the black dragon in Donglai 東萊; Gu Yong 谷永 submitting a memorial on the solar eclipse on the New Year's Day (sanzhao); Kong Guang 孔光 citing the frequent occurrences of wind and thunder as verification; and Cai Yong 蔡邕 replying [to questions on anomalies, though a few words appear omitted at the column break?][?]—critics do not carefully select what is valid in their words, but lumped them together with the practitioners of prognostication charts (tuchen) and numerology (shushu), superficially dismissing and casting them aside as useless. Is that not going much too far!

Therefore, I have maintained that the Han dynasty, being close to antiquity, possessed the inherited learning of the "Great Plan" (Hongfan) and the Spring and Autumn Annals. From imperial decrees and edicts above down to memorials and deliberations below, all had the means to comprehend the connection between Heaven and humanity and to know whence disasters and ominous vapors arose; ruler and ministers sighed in concern and changed countenance, taking them as warnings. What is meant by "dwelling high in the majestic court yet taking thought for the four quarters, gazing upon a thousand ages past so as to mirror the present era, and knowing the Way of Heaven without stepping outside one's door" was possible because this learning still existed.

The Book of Changes (Yi) says: "Heaven hangs out its images, revealing good and ill fortune, and the sage models himself upon them." It also says: "Observe the patterns of Heaven to examine the changes of the times." Thus, the Way of the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity) is not easy to speak of. Their numinous principles ride upon emptiness and communicate with one another; their spiritual qi revolves and presses upon one another. Humanity dwells in the midst of Heaven and Earth just like a dragon in the heavens, …

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
徹內外無非天也者如魚在水徹內外無
非水也者有動必應有兆必著其幾甚微
其效甚徑神明之事可以智巧得乎聲以
同應氣以類感蜀鍾鳴而銅山崩瑤樞散
而地維裂柔風至而酒盈蠶絲舍而弦絕
物之相物焉可誣也陽燧在掌太陽火方
珠運握少陰水太白暉而雞夜號介駟動
而鼉鳴野精之相應無所待也瞽師奏音
風雨暴至庶女籲天雷電下擊拊標而炎
===
霜飛揮戈而羲馭迴專精厲意上通于天
也五雲之變可望豐成八風之朝可考吉
祥天臺玉策之占農師賈豎之智其於觀
天行一也古之大聖精神燭萬物動靜諧
陰陽與天地參光鬼神齊靈察幾明物不
失纖微況於人乎是故傳圖書以示重襲
龜策以待事樹靈臺以觀象陳嶰管以測
氣聆鳴絃以審聲順八絃以聽政夫孰非
以燮調在我旁稽于五事之徵哉傳曰春
punctuated: 徹內外無非天也者；如魚在水，徹內外無非水也者。有動必應，有兆必著，其幾甚微，其效甚徑，神明之事，可以智巧得乎？聲以同應，氣以類感。蜀鍾鳴而銅山崩，瑤樞散而地維裂，柔風至而酒盈，蠶絲舍而弦絕，物之相物，焉可誣也？陽燧在掌，太陽火；方珠運握，少陰水；太白暉而雞夜號，介駟動而鼉鳴野，精之相應，無所待也。瞽師奏音，風雨暴至；庶女籲天，雷電下擊；拊標而炎霜飛，揮戈而羲馭迴，專精厲意，上通于天也。五雲之變，可望豐成；八風之朝，可考吉祥。天臺玉策之占，農師賈豎之智，其於觀天行，一也。古之大聖，精神燭萬物，動靜諧陰陽，與天地參光，鬼神齊靈，察幾明物，不失纖微，況於人乎？是故傳圖書以示重，襲龜策以待事，樹靈臺以觀象，陳嶰管以測氣，聆鳴絃以審聲，順八絃以聽政，夫孰非以燮調在我，旁稽于五事之徵哉？傳曰：「春
translation_en: …pervading both within and without, there is nothing that is not the sky; or like a fish in the water, pervading both within and without, there is nothing that is not water. Where there is movement, there is inevitably a response; where there is an omen, it inevitably becomes manifest. Its subtle springs are extremely minute, yet its effects are remarkably direct. How could the affairs of spiritual intelligence be grasped through mere cleverness and artifice? Sounds respond to what is of the same pitch, and vital energies (qi) are moved by what is of the same kind. When the bell in Shu rang, the Copper Mountain collapsed; when the Jade Pivot star scattered, the cords of the earth cracked; when the gentle breeze arrives, the wine brims over; when the silkworm spins its silk [in the mouth], the musical string snaps. When things correspond to other things, how can this be denied? Hold a burning-mirror in the palm, and fire comes from the Great Yang [the sun]; turn a square-pearl mirror in the grasp, and water comes from the Lesser Yin [the moon]; when Venus shines brightly, roosters crow in the night; when the Armored Four-Horse star moves, alligators bellow in the wilds—the mutual resonance of essences waits upon nothing external. When the blind music master played his notes, wind and rain suddenly arrived; when the commoner woman cried out to Heaven, thunder and lightning struck down; when one struck his chest [in grief], summer frost flew; when one brandished his halberd, the chariot of the sun turned back—such focused essence and fierce intent communicated upward to Heaven. From the transformations of the five-colored clouds, one can hope for an abundant harvest; on the mornings of the eight winds, one can examine auspicious signs. The divinations of the imperial observatory and jade tallies, and the practical wisdom of veteran farmers and merchant lads, are one and the same when it comes to observing the movements of Heaven. The great sages of antiquity illuminated all things with their spirit, harmonized their movement and stillness with yin and yang, matched the radiance of Heaven and Earth, equaled the numinous efficacy of ghosts and spirits, and perceived subtle springs and understood things without missing the slightest fraction—how much more so in the realm of human affairs! Therefore, they transmitted the River Chart and Luo Writing to show their weight, consulted both tortoise-shell and milfoil divination to await affairs, erected the Numinous Terrace to observe celestial phenomena, set out the pitch-pipes of Xie Valley to measure the seasonal vital energies, listened to sounding strings to examine tones, and followed the eight directions [eight cords of the earth] in administering governance. Which of these was not done because the responsibility for harmonizing and regulating rests within oneself, while broadly verifying it against the signs of the Five Demeanors? A commentary says: "The Spring…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
秋舉往以明來視天下有物與之同其比
者通倫類以貫其理則國家之事粲然可
知又曰王者尊天地重陰陽知王治之象
名之曰經考見天心則詩書易春秋禮樂
皆是物也故洚水懷山堯舜疇咨桑穀生
庭太戊修德鼎耳雊雉高宗正事大風作
而成以出郊旱魃甚而宣以側身古人未
發詞陳令天心顧懷者由天人之際素明
炳而精與之一也儻不其然湯之六事六
===
言纔脫於口四方之風湊千里之雨至宋
景片善出乎身妖躔退伏出三言獲三賞
星退三舍子韋得一一預知之然則天人
之際亦不遠矣古之人于陰陽五行必有
學矣奈何其諱言之也宋儒陸九淵蔡沈
二子以謂讖緯小技不足知天道適以啓
邪說亂常經故言春秋不著事應洪範五
行不必一一求其配蓋以杜後世之惑耳
陳誼甚正非書生敢議竊聞之惟天至虛
punctuated: 秋舉往以明來，視天下有物與之同其比者，通倫類以貫其理，則國家之事粲然可知。」又曰：「王者尊天地，重陰陽，知王治之象，名之曰經。」考見天心，則《詩》、《書》、《易》、《春秋》、《禮》、《樂》，皆是物也。故洚水懷山，堯、舜疇咨；桑穀生庭，太戊修德；鼎耳雊雉，高宗正事；大風作而成以出郊；旱魃甚而宣以側身。古人未發詞陳令，天心顧懷者，由天人之際素明炳而精與之一也。儻不其然，湯之六事六言，纔脫於口，四方之風湊，千里之雨至；宋景片善出乎身，妖躔退伏，出三言獲三賞，星退三舍，子韋得一一預知之。然則天人之際亦不遠矣。古之人于陰陽五行，必有學矣，奈何其諱言之也？宋儒陸九淵、蔡沈二子，以謂讖緯小技，不足知天道，適以啓邪說、亂常經，故言《春秋》不著事應，《洪範》五行不必一一求其配，蓋以杜後世之惑耳。陳誼甚正，非書生敢議。竊聞之，惟天至虛，
translation_en: … the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) cites the past to illuminate the future; observing things in the world that share similar analogies, it connects categories and classes to thread through their principles, so that the affairs of the state can be clearly known." It also says: "A true king reveres Heaven and Earth, values yin and yang, and understands the emblems of kingly governance, naming them the Classics." When we examine them to discern the mind of Heaven, the Odes (Shi), Documents (Shu), Changes (Yi), Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), Rites (Li), and Music (Yue) are all this very thing. Therefore, when the floodwaters encompassed the mountains, Yao and Shun anxiously consulted their ministers; when mulberry and paper-mulberry trees grew together in the court, Taiwu cultivated his virtue; when a pheasant crowed on the ear of a tripod, Gaozong rectified his affairs; when a great wind arose, King Cheng went out to the suburban altar; and when the drought demon raged fiercely, King Xuan humbled himself in self-reproach. That the mind of Heaven looked upon the ancients with care even before they had uttered words or issued ordinances was because the relationship between Heaven and humankind had always been brightly manifest to them, and their essential spirit was one with it. Were it not so, how could it be that when Tang's six self-reproaches and six words had barely left his mouth, winds converged from all four quarters and rain fell across a thousand li? Or that when a single virtuous thought arose from the person of Duke Jing of Song, the baleful planet retreated—uttering three statements, he reaped three rewards, the planet withdrew three zodiacal lodges, and Ziwei was able to foretell each one in advance? Thus the nexus between Heaven and humankind is not far off at all. The ancients must have had a true learning regarding yin, yang, and the Five Phases; why then should one shy away from speaking of it? The two Song Confucian masters Lu Jiuyuan 陸九淵 and Cai Shen 蔡沈 held that prognostication and apocrypha (chenwei) were petty techniques insufficient for knowing the Way of Heaven, serving only to open the door to heterodox doctrines and throw the constant Classics into confusion; hence they argued that the Spring and Autumn Annals does not record portentous responses to events, and that in the Five Phases of the "Great Plan" (Hongfan) one need not seek one-to-one correspondences for everything. This was meant simply to shut off delusion in later ages. The principles they set forth are most upright, and not something a mere scholar would dare to criticize. Yet I have humbly heard that Heaven is utterly vacuous, …

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
森列萬靈惟大君大聖尤與萬靈相接精
液所朝夕氣息所呼吸天帝所鑒觀而神
響所豐融也焉有一動靜而不關天鑒者
乎焉有一譴告而不由治象者乎昔之儒
者憂其鑿吾猶慮夫不知天而不畏也故
易之卦氣如閉關施誥作樂育物之屬無
不與天和叅配月令之說蓋宗之春秋所
書即一飛鳥昆蟲之異謹而錄之以明王
事詩書言天無時可離無事不應尤詳於
===
君德若色脉徵而五臟之虛盈無謬焉若
呈貌盡相而鑑中之影先至焉經義之應
明白甚矣世儒言天則曰仁愛人主言災
應則拱手稱玄遠而不敢知邵氏之皇極
蔡氏之洪範則醇之箕子之庶徵則疑之
漢史漢儒之論則藩而外之然則天在有
無之間耶人主宜何從焉今夫孝子事親
起敬起孝不敢問喜怒所由此自誠理宜
爾也及其怒也必曰我罪伊何曰於我何
punctuated: 森列萬靈，惟大君、大聖尤與萬靈相接，精液所朝夕，氣息所呼吸，天帝所鑒觀，而神響所豐融也。焉有一動靜而不關天鑒者乎？焉有一譴告而不由治象者乎？昔之儒者憂其鑿，吾猶慮夫不知天而不畏也。故《易》之卦氣，如閉關、施誥、作樂、育物之屬，無不與天和叅配，《月令》之說蓋宗之。《春秋》所書，即一飛鳥、昆蟲之異，謹而錄之，以明王事。《詩》《書》言天，無時可離，無事不應，尤詳於君德，若色脉徵而五臟之虛盈無謬焉，若呈貌盡相而鑑中之影先至焉，經義之應明白甚矣。世儒言天則曰仁愛人主，言災應則拱手稱玄遠而不敢知；邵氏之《皇極》、蔡氏之《洪範》則醇之，箕子之庶徵則疑之，漢史、漢儒之論則藩而外之。然則天在有無之間耶？人主宜何從焉？今夫孝子事親，起敬起孝，不敢問喜怒所由，此自誠理宜爾也；及其怒也，必曰「我罪伊何」，曰「於我何
translation_en: … arrayed with myriad spirits; yet only the great sovereign and the great sage are especially in communion with the myriad spirits. What their vital essence attends to morning and evening, and what their breath inhales and exhales, is what the Lord of Heaven observes and inspects, and where spiritual echoes abound in harmony. How could there be a single movement or stillness that does not concern Heaven's inspection? How could there be a single reprimand or warning that does not arise from the state of governance? Scholars of the past worried that such interpretations were forced, yet I rather worry that people will fail to know Heaven and thus not stand in awe of it. Therefore, in the hexagram qi of the Book of Changes (Yi), matters such as closing the passes, issuing proclamations, making music, and nurturing things are without exception matched and coordinated with heavenly harmony; the doctrines of the Monthly Ordinances (Yueling) were in fact modeled on this. In what the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records, even an anomaly involving a single flying bird or insect was carefully registered in order to illuminate the affairs of the king. When the Book of Odes (Shi) and the Book of Documents (Shu) speak of Heaven, there is no moment when it can be parted from, and no affair to which it does not respond, being especially detailed regarding the sovereign's virtue—just as when complexion and pulse give signs, there is no mistake about the depletion or fullness of the five viscera; and just as when one presents one's countenance in full form, the reflection in the mirror arrives first. The correspondences in the meaning of the Classics are clear indeed! When contemporary scholars speak of Heaven, they say it benevolently loves the ruler of men, yet when they speak of the correspondences of disasters, they fold their hands, call them abstruse and distant, and dare not claim to know them. They regard Shao Yong's Supreme Ultimate (Huangji) and Cai Shen's Great Plan (Hongfan) as pure, yet doubt Jizi's "various verifications" (shuzheng), and fence off and exclude the discussions of the Han histories and Han scholars. If so, does Heaven exist somewhere between being and non-being? What should the ruler of men follow? Now, when a filial son serves his parents, he arouses reverence and filiality, not daring to question the source of their pleasure or anger—this is naturally how sincere principle ought to be. Yet when they become angry, he must say, "What is my offense?" and say, "What have I …"

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
哉君事天亦子道耳則夫怒所由起安可
不知所從而修之而弭之乎人主誠覽大
易之吉凶察洪範之休咎採春秋之災異
考詩書之天道深惟仁愛之心法古懼思
之意原兩漢君臣之際對時順令以應經
義一切政刑非時苛紊傷陰陽之和戕萬
物之性者宜以類求而去之使敬天一念
不爲減膳撤樂之文而實有爕和補捄之
政庶徵福極可使還至立效也雖然禆竈
===
梓慎之術世以爲禁生何敢與聞事乃丙
魏事君惓惓之義竊以謂後世儒者所未
及而顧有言焉
第三問
沈學
同考試官教諭曹　批〔用法之弊與用人之道是策條對無遺鑿鑿有據不獨其文之美也〕
同考試官學正祝　批〔譚時務如指掌而調復高古得人若子知不肆於法者〕
punctuated:
哉」？君事天，亦子道耳。則夫怒所由起，安可不知所從，而修之而弭之乎？人主誠覽《大易》之吉凶，察《洪範》之休咎，採《春秋》之災異，考《詩》、《書》之天道，深惟仁愛之心，法古懼思之意，原兩漢君臣之際，對時順令，以應經義。一切政刑非時苛紊、傷陰陽之和、戕萬物之性者，宜以類求而去之。使敬天一念，不爲減膳撤樂之文，而實有爕和補捄之政，庶徵福極，可使還至立效也。雖然，禆竈、梓慎之術，世以爲禁，生何敢與聞？事乃丙、魏事君惓惓之義，竊以謂後世儒者所未及，而顧有言焉。

第三問
沈學
同考試官教諭曹　批〔用法之弊與用人之道，是策條對無遺，鑿鑿有據，不獨其文之美也。〕
同考試官學正祝　批〔譚時務如指掌，而調復高古。得人若子，知不肆於法者，〕
translation_en:
… With me?" A ruler serving Heaven is likewise simply following the Way of a son. When anger arises, how then can one fail to know whence it comes, so as to cultivate oneself and avert it? If the sovereign truly examines the good and bad fortune in the Great Changes (Dayi), observes the auspicious and inauspicious signs in the "Grand Norm" ("Hongfan"), gathers the portents and anomalies of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), investigates the Way of Heaven in the Odes (Shi) and the Documents (Shu), deeply reflects upon Heaven's benevolent love, emulates the ancient intent of fearful self-examination, and traces the relations between ruler and minister in the Former and Later Han, he will match the seasons and accord with the monthly ordinances so as to correspond to the principles of the Classics. All governance and punishments that are ill-timed, harsh, or disorderly—injuring the harmony of yin and yang and harming the nature of the myriad things—should be sought out by category and eliminated. Thus, if the single thought of revering Heaven does not remain the mere formality of reducing the imperial table and suspending music, but instead results in actual governance that harmonizes and remedies, then the "various verifications" and the "five blessings" of the Supreme Ultimate can be made to return swiftly and take immediate effect. Even so, the arts of Pi Zao 禆竈 and Zi Shen 梓慎 are regarded by the world as forbidden; how would this student dare to meddle in them? Yet as for the earnest devotion with which Bing Ji 丙吉 and Wei Xiang 魏相 served their ruler, I venture to think that Confucian scholars of later ages have not matched it, and therefore I have presumed to speak of it here.

Third Policy Question
Shen Xue 沈學
Associate Examiner Instructor Cao 曹 comments: [On the abuses in applying the laws and the Way of employing men, this policy essay answers item by item without omission, with solid and well-founded evidence; it is not merely admirable for the beauty of its prose.]
Associate Examiner Subprefectural Instructor Zhu 祝 comments: [He discusses current affairs as clearly as pointing to the palm of one's hand, and his style is moreover lofty and archaic. In obtaining a man such as you, we know you are one who will not be reckless with the laws; …]

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
國家有賴矣
同考試官敎授錢　批〔用人乃〕
國家第一急務而世每以拘攣之見限格才俊致有結束之患篇中欲稍寛文法使人人得
〔以自見是留心於用人者且文更軽瞻有體錄之〕
考試官修撰沈　批〔用人者爲文法所拘此以有才難之嘆也〕
〔是策援据精覈亦復敢言豈所謂識時務者哉〕
考試官左賛善沈　批〔敷對詳明以嘗留心世務者錄之〕
天下之材不同而上之所以任之者亦異
夫世有中材有豪傑豪傑之性安於善則
===
無務以法繩之法太急則英鋭萎索而約
結之嘆起中材之性善惡混則必務以法
閑之法太弛則精略厭倦而競勸之意微
二者雖殊其不足以得人均也夫何以稱
之曰豪傑也葢其裁慮足以理糾棼强忍
足以投艱大應卒則談咲指麾而跡不膠
居成則收名歛筴而善不伐煦乎有極溺
噓枯之仁浩乎有併包囊括之量此品之
上也下此則畜德未深晰幾未朗工於爲
punctuated:
國家有賴矣。
同考試官敎授錢　批〔用人乃〕國家第一急務，而世每以拘攣之見限格才俊，致有結束之患。篇中欲稍寛文法，使人人得〔以自見，是留心於用人者。且文更軽瞻有體，錄之。〕
考試官修撰沈　批〔用人者爲文法所拘，此以有「才難」之嘆也。〕〔是策援据精覈，亦復敢言，豈所謂識時務者哉？〕
考試官左賛善沈　批〔敷對詳明，以嘗留心世務者，錄之。〕
天下之材不同，而上之所以任之者亦異。夫世有中材，有豪傑。豪傑之性安於善，則無務以法繩之；法太急則英鋭萎索，而約結之嘆起。中材之性善惡混，則必務以法閑之；法太弛則精略厭倦，而競勸之意微。二者雖殊，其不足以得人均也。夫何以稱之曰豪傑也？葢其裁慮足以理糾棼，强忍足以投艱大；應卒則談咲指麾而跡不膠，居成則收名歛筴而善不伐。煦乎有極溺噓枯之仁，浩乎有併包囊括之量，此品之上也。下此則畜德未深，晰幾未朗，工於爲
translation_en:
…the state will have someone to rely upon.
Associate Examiner Instructor Qian comments: Employing men is the foremost urgent task of the state, yet the world constantly restricts talented men with cramped views, resulting in the malady of fettering them. In this essay, the candidate wishes to slightly relax the legalistic regulations so that everyone is able to distinguish himself; he is someone who pays close attention to the employment of men. Moreover, the writing is agile, rich [?], and well-structured. Record it for publication.
Examiner Senior Compiler Shen comments: Those who employ men are bound by legalistic regulations, which is why there is the lament that "talent is hard to find." This policy essay cites evidence with precision and thoroughness, and also speaks boldly—is he not what is called one who understands the affairs of the times?
Examiner Left Admonisher Shen comments: The exposition and response are detailed and clear, as from one who has paid close attention to worldly affairs. Record it for publication.
The talents of the empire are not uniform, and the means by which superiors employ them also differ. Now, in the world there are men of mediocre talent and there are heroes. The nature of heroes rests comfortably in goodness, so there is no need to bind them with laws; if the laws are too stringent, their heroic spirit withers away, and laments over being constrained and tied down arise. The nature of men of mediocre talent is a mixture of good and bad, so one must make it a point to restrain them with laws; if the laws are too lax, their diligence and planning grow weary, and their resolve to strive and be encouraged diminishes. Although the two cases are different, their failure to secure the right men is the same. Now, why are they called heroes? It is because their judgment and deliberation are sufficient to untangle complexities, and their fortitude and endurance are sufficient to take on great and difficult tasks; when responding to sudden emergencies, they direct affairs while talking and laughing, without getting bogged down in fixed routines; when dwelling in success, they withdraw from fame and fold up their plans without boasting of their merits. Warmly, they possess the benevolence to rescue the drowning and breathe life into the withered; vastly, they possess the capacity to embrace and encompass all. This is the highest class of men. Below this, their accumulation of virtue is not yet deep, and their discernment of subtle incipient tendencies is not yet clear; they are skillful at…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
謀而或拙於立斷明於記憶而或暗於設
施守一寄則有餘兼衆委則不足持文墨
則雍容運籌鈐則鹵莽斯則性有所偏才
有所滯善用之可以成不善用可以敗成
則展其能以見於世而上之法行敗則壞
其能以棄於世而下之情阻故馭中材與
豪傑異而用人者不可不察也古之陶冶
人羣者以所當加之法而嚴之於循常襲
故之流以所不必加之意而寬之於瓌瑋
卓犖之士其用之也夢卜師相屠販公卿
一切恩仇疎戚不少芥蔕於中非簡節也
以非法之所能揖摶也其核之也辨以八
法正以六敘使百司庶府弭耳抑心鰓鰓
然奉上之奔走而不敢肆非厚防也以非
法不足以綰結之也故天下有法內之材
廢法不可也有法外之材徒法不可也而
操縱張弛之權吾因人以酌之而已夫三
代以前遐哉邈乎無容贅矣姑以晚近言
punctuated: 謀而或拙於立斷，明於記憶而或暗於設施，守一寄則有餘，兼衆委則不足，持文墨則雍容，運籌鈐則鹵莽。斯則性有所偏，才有所滯，善用之可以成，不善用可以敗。成則展其能以見於世，而上之法行；敗則壞其能以棄於世，而下之情阻。故馭中材與豪傑異，而用人者不可不察也。古之陶冶人羣者，以所當加之法，而嚴之於循常襲故之流；以所不必加之意，而寬之於瓌瑋卓犖之士。其用之也，夢卜師相，屠販公卿，一切恩仇疎戚，不少芥蔕於中，非簡節也，以非法之所能揖摶也。其核之也，辨以八法，正以六敘，使百司庶府弭耳抑心，鰓鰓然奉上之奔走而不敢肆，非厚防也，以非法不足以綰結之也。故天下有法內之材，廢法不可也；有法外之材，徒法不可也。而操縱張弛之權，吾因人以酌之而已。夫三代以前，遐哉邈乎，無容贅矣；姑以晚近言
translation_en:
…devise plans, yet perhaps be clumsy at making immediate decisions; they may be bright in memory, yet perhaps be in the dark when it comes to practical implementation; they may have more than enough capacity to guard a single charge, yet fall short when taking on multiple commissions; they may be poised and graceful when wielding brush and ink, yet rash and crude when conducting strategic planning and military command. In such cases, their natures have their biases and their talents have their limitations; if employed well they can succeed, whereas if employed poorly they can fail. When they succeed, they unfold their abilities to manifest them in the world, and the sovereign's laws are carried out; when they fail, they ruin their abilities and are cast aside by the world, and the sentiments of those below are obstructed. Therefore, managing men of medium talent differs from managing extraordinary heroes, and those who employ men cannot fail to examine this.

When the ancients molded the multitude of men, they took the laws that ought to be applied and enforced them strictly upon the sort who merely follow routine and tread old paths; and they took the scrutiny that need not be applied and showed leniency toward magnificent and towering scholars. In employing the latter, they found preceptors and chief councilors through dreams and divination, and raised up dukes and ministers from among butchers and peddlers; all matters of favor or enmity, distance or kinship, left not the slightest thorn in their minds. This was not out of negligence toward rules, but because such men cannot be gathered and bound together by mere laws. In verifying the former, they distinguished them by the Eight Regulations and rectified them by the Six Ranks, causing the hundred offices and myriad bureaus to flatten their ears and restrain their hearts, anxiously hastening at the service of their superiors without daring to act wantonly. This was not out of excessive precaution, but because without laws it is impossible to bind and hold them together. Therefore, in the realm there are talents within the scope of the law, for whom abolishing the law will not do; and there are talents beyond the scope of the law, for whom relying solely on the law will not do. As for the authority to rein in or give free rein, to tighten or to relax, we simply weigh and adjust it according to the person.

Now, the era before the Three Dynasties is far and distant indeed, and there is no need to speak of it at length; if we provisionally speak of more recent times…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之則魏漢數君不猶可考而鏡乎昔樂羊
爲魏文侯將三年始拔中山文侯封之靈
壽樂羊跪而辭曰臣攻中山有謗臣於大
王者謗書盈篋大王終不信之故臣得拔
中山此乃大王之功非臣之功也若文侯
者可謂能信賢矣陳平事漢於傾側擾攘
之際請捐黃金行反間高祖乃出四萬斤
與之恣所爲不問出入後果數設秘計斃
范亡項走狄禽韓佐勃誅呂爲漢伊周若
===
高祖者可謂能用智矣汲黯在武帝時爲
謁者上使往視河內火還報曰家人失火
比屋延燒不足憂臣過河內貧人傷水旱
萬餘家或父子相食臣謹以便宜持節發
河內倉粟以賑貧民請歸節伏矯制罪上
賢而釋之若武帝者可謂能行義矣趙充
國受宣帝命亟擊先零充國計在招降令
諸豪皆解遂罷騎兵上留田十二事卽璽
書三問堅持不顧廷議皆以後將軍言是
punctuated: 之，則魏、漢數君，不猶可考而鏡乎？昔樂羊爲魏文侯將，三年始拔中山，文侯封之靈壽。樂羊跪而辭曰：「臣攻中山，有謗臣於大王者，謗書盈篋，大王終不信之，故臣得拔中山。此乃大王之功，非臣之功也。」若文侯者，可謂能信賢矣。陳平事漢，於傾側擾攘之際，請捐黃金行反間，高祖乃出四萬斤與之，恣所爲，不問出入。後果數設秘計，斃范、亡項、走狄、禽韓，佐勃誅呂，爲漢伊、周。若高祖者，可謂能用智矣。汲黯在武帝時爲謁者，上使往視河內火。還報曰：「家人失火，比屋延燒，不足憂。臣過河內，貧人傷水旱萬餘家，或父子相食。臣謹以便宜，持節發河內倉粟以賑貧民。請歸節，伏矯制罪。」上賢而釋之。若武帝者，可謂能行義矣。趙充國受宣帝命，亟擊先零。充國計在招降，令諸豪皆解，遂罷騎兵，上留田十二事，卽璽書三問，堅持不顧。廷議皆以後將軍言是，…
translation_en:
… of them, can those several rulers of Wei and Han not still be examined and taken as a mirror? In the past, Yue Yang 樂羊 served as general for Marquis Wen of Wei 魏文侯; only after three years did he capture Zhongshan 中山, and Marquis Wen enfeoffed him at Lingshou 靈壽. Yue Yang knelt and declined, saying: "While your servant was attacking Zhongshan, there were those who slandered your servant to Your Majesty; the letters of slander filled a chest, yet Your Majesty refused to believe them to the end, and therefore your servant was able to capture Zhongshan. This is Your Majesty's achievement, not your servant's achievement." One such as Marquis Wen may be said to have been able to trust the worthy.

When Chen Ping 陳平 served Han amidst a time of peril and turmoil, he asked to spend gold to sow discord among the enemy. Gaozu 高祖 thereupon brought out forty thousand catties and gave it to him, letting him do as he pleased without asking about his expenditures. Later, as expected, he repeatedly devised secret stratagems, bringing about the death of Fan [Zeng 范增], destroying Xiang [Yu 項羽], driving off the northern tribes (Di 狄), capturing Han [Xin 韓信], and assisting [Zhou] Bo 周勃 in executing the Lü 呂 clan, becoming an Yi [Yin 伊尹] or Duke of Zhou 周公 for the Han. One such as Gaozu may be said to have been able to employ the wise.

During the time of Emperor Wu 武帝, Ji An 汲黯 served as an Internuncio (Yezhe 謁者), and the Emperor sent him to go and inspect a fire in Henei 河內. Returning, he reported: "Commoners accidentally started a fire and the adjacent houses caught the blaze, which is not worth worrying about. When your servant passed through Henei, poor people suffering from floods and droughts numbered over ten thousand households, some even to the point of fathers and sons eating one another. Your servant ventured to act as the situation demanded, using my imperial insignia to open the granaries of Henei to relieve the impoverished people. I beg to return my insignia and submit to punishment for forging an imperial decree." The Emperor considered him worthy and pardoned him. One such as Emperor Wu may be said to have been able to practice righteousness.

Zhao Chongguo 趙充國 received Emperor Xuan's 宣帝 command to swiftly attack the Xianlian 先零 [Qiang]. Chongguo's plan lay in inducing their surrender and causing the various chieftains to disperse; he thereupon withdrew the cavalry and submitted twelve proposals for establishing garrison farms (tuntian 留田). Even when questioned three times by imperial rescript, he held firm to his position without wavering. Once the court conference all considered the General of the Rear's (Hou Jiangjun 後將軍) words to be right …

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
可用卒之羗虜破壞坐收全勝之功若宣
帝者可謂能任計矣夫積毀至危機也捐
金不計出入至難明也矯制涉於擅至抗
上也留田疑於懦至玩敵也向使四臣無
深知之主而據迹者後以三尺隨其後安
知玩敵不從李法抗上不下廷尉乎捐數
萬金不疑乾没積毀不中奇禍乎蓋古人
謀必裨之於國而不計一身之安危治必
要之於終而不恤一時之謗議故形迹可
疑而嫌釁常略也豪傑之士所以名成而
不隳功立而不磯者大都若此矣洪惟我
===
太祖高皇帝以一旅渡江而闢
乾坤於再位
成祖文皇帝以偏師南指而滌
日月於重明當是時英彥景從異能雲集將經
百戰之餘士奇千載之遇而
二祖又能綜鑒人倫區較材品飴荼別於嘗試
利鈍審於剸裁破拘攣之網而奬奇儁批
punctuated: 可用，卒之羗虜破壞，坐收全勝之功。若宣帝者，可謂能任計矣。夫積毀，至危機也；捐金不計出入，至難明也；矯制涉於擅，至抗上也；留田疑於懦，至玩敵也。向使四臣無深知之主，而據迹者後以三尺隨其後，安知玩敵不從李法，抗上不下廷尉乎？捐數萬金不疑乾没，積毀不中奇禍乎？蓋古人謀必裨之於國，而不計一身之安危；治必要之於終，而不恤一時之謗議。故形迹可疑，而嫌釁常略也。豪傑之士所以名成而不隳，功立而不磯者，大都若此矣。洪惟我太祖高皇帝以一旅渡江，而闢乾坤於再位；成祖文皇帝以偏師南指，而滌日月於重明。當是時，英彥景從，異能雲集，將經百戰之餘，士奇千載之遇，而二祖又能綜鑒人倫，區較材品，飴荼別於嘗試，利鈍審於剸裁，破拘攣之網而奬奇儁，批
translation_en:
… ought to be adopted. In the end, the Qiang caitiffs were broken and destroyed, and he effortlessly reaped the merit of a complete victory. Someone like Emperor Xuan may truly be said to have been able to entrust men with strategic planning!

Now, accumulating slander is the ultimate peril; expending gold without accounting for receipts and outlays is the hardest thing to explain; forging an imperial decree borders on usurpation and is the ultimate defiance of the sovereign; and staying behind to establish state farms invites suspicion of cowardice and is the ultimate trifling with the enemy. Suppose those four ministers had not had sovereigns who understood them deeply, and those who judge merely by outward traces had come after them with the three-foot statutory code—how do we know that for trifling with the enemy one would not have been subjected to military law [Li fa], or that for defying the sovereign one would not have been handed down to the Chamberlain for Law Enforcement (Tingwei)? That expending tens of thousands in gold would not have incurred suspicion of embezzlement, or that accumulated slander would not have brought on an extraordinary disaster? Indeed, when the ancients laid plans, they sought only to benefit the state without calculating their own personal safety or peril; in governing, they looked always to the final outcome without heeding temporary slanders and criticisms. Thus, even when outward traces were open to suspicion, causes for jealousy and rift were routinely overlooked. The reason heroic andoutstanding men were able to achieve fame without having it ruined, and establish merit without being thwarted [? 磯], was largely like this.

Vast indeed was our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu, the Hongwu Emperor), who crossed the Yangtze with a single brigade and opened up heaven and earth to set the throne anew; and the Accomplished Progenitor, Emperor Wen (Chengzu, the Yongle Emperor), who pointed southward with a detachment of troops and cleansed the sun and moon to restore their double brilliance! At that time, outstanding talents followed like shadows and extraordinary abilities gathered like clouds; generals came through the aftermath of a hundred battles, and scholars marveled at an encounter found once in a thousand years. Moreover, the Two Progenitors were able comprehensively to mirror human character and distinguish and compare grades of talent: sweet malt and bitter sow-thistle were differentiated through actual tasting, and sharpness and bluntness were discerned through decisive cutting. They broke through the nets of petty constraint to encourage extraordinary heroes, struck aside…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
雌黃之口而表樸椎解牽制之紲而掖跰
弛樹勸駕之幟而旌鄉往以故良駑不竝
羈勇怯不混縶而得人之盛馭士之法信
有非漢魏數君所能彷彿其萬一者矣然
歷世旣久操用人之柄者閒或有乏才之
嘆又何以故哉愚念此至熟已蓋
國步初夷則規創必密
甲令已定則事體素安廸其弊也
朝廷守積常之勢而厭釐更官司狃苟且之
===
風而習窳惰人窮於法而卮詞粃事者興
矣法束其才而尫全韋護者出矣由是上
之用下多據趨舍以任見聞下之罔上每
狥耳目以匿形迹衆違而獨從之輒嫌愼
忮而息喙衆可而獨否之率愳娼嫉而引
躬期會苟失蝮吏設穽待之矣得無惴乎
端緒方成簧口從旁議之矣能無撓乎顯
譽不可以屢邀人將吹洗其瘢疵而排之
孰與寧失譽而全身膚功不可以屢奏人
punctuated: 雌黃之口而表樸椎，解牽制之紲而掖跰弛，樹勸駕之幟而旌鄉往。以故良駑不竝羈，勇怯不混縶，而得人之盛、馭士之法，信有非漢、魏數君所能彷彿其萬一者矣。然歷世旣久，操用人之柄者閒或有乏才之嘆，又何以故哉？愚念此至熟已。蓋國步初夷，則規創必密；甲令已定，則事體素安。廸其弊也，朝廷守積常之勢而厭釐更，官司狃苟且之風而習窳惰。人窮於法，而卮詞粃事者興矣；法束其才，而尫全韋護者出矣。由是上之用下，多據趨舍以任見聞；下之罔上，每狥耳目以匿形迹。衆違而獨從之，輒嫌愼忮而息喙；衆可而獨否之，率愳娼嫉而引躬。期會苟失，蝮吏設穽待之矣，得無惴乎？端緒方成，簧口從旁議之矣，能無撓乎？顯譽不可以屢邀，人將吹洗其瘢疵而排之，孰與寧失譽而全身？膚功不可以屢奏，人
translation_en: … the mouths of carping critics and highlighted the plain and unadorned; they untied the leashes of restraint and raised up the unbridled and unconventional; they planted the banner of encouragement and honored those who inclined toward service. For this reason, fine steeds and nags were not haltered together, the brave and the timid were not tethered without distinction, and the abundance of talent obtained as well as the methods for managing scholars truly were such that those several rulers of Han and Wei could not even approximate one ten-thousandth of them! Yet after many generations have passed, those who hold the handle of employing men occasionally sigh over a lack of talent—why is this so? I have pondered this most thoroughly. Indeed, when the fortunes of the state are first pacified, the founding regulations must be comprehensive; when the primary statutes have been settled, the conduct of affairs is habitually peaceful. Following the course of its abuses, the Court holds to the momentum of accumulated routine and dislikes reform and change, while officialdom grows accustomed to a culture of perfunctoriness and becomes habituated to laziness and sloth. When men are hemmed in by regulations, those who offer empty rhetoric and botch actual affairs arise; when regulations bind their talents, those who seek feeble self-preservation and pliable protection emerge. Consequently, in employing subordinates, superiors mostly rely on conventional preferences and trust to superficial hearsay; in deceiving superiors, subordinates constantly cater to eyes and ears in order to conceal their true tracks. If the multitude opposes something and one alone follows it, one immediately fears resentment and hostility [?] and holds one's tongue; if the multitude approves something and one alone rejects it, one generally dreads jealous malice and withdraws oneself. If a deadline or accounting is missed, viperous clerks set pitfalls and wait for one—how can one not tremble in fear? When the initial threads of an undertaking are just taking shape, glib tongues criticize it from the sidelines—how can one not be thwarted? Illustrious renown cannot be repeatedly sought, for others will blow apart the hair to wash out one's scars and blemishes and push one aside; how does that compare to preferring to forfeit renown and preserve one's person? Great achievements cannot be repeatedly presented to the throne, for others …

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
又枝蔓其細瑣而蔽之孰與寧棄功而免
患無惑乎宵人負靑而營窟局士信節以
守株盲者處暗而譚離婁之明躄者端坐
而矜許少之捷貌羊質以虎皮飾鴞鳴以
鳳釆本體愈不可識而沉痼益以眩人上
下相貿豪傑何由而顯乎所謂草昧之初
恒多賢熈洽之後常乏才者語不誣也
明興
列聖重光治化汪濊我
===
皇上以冲睿繼統用人行政鋭意興修
二祖之軌頊憂士習稍媮治理踳駁
特申禁令飭學校嚴評汰復久任精覈之政瑩
然烈於往古而疆圉介冑能秉障破敵抵
掌籌邊旋起徒步建大將一時
德意所敷薄海風靡文武吏士莫不盱衡而肩
當世之務投筆而修羽檄之功豈患乏才
哉第愚竊有異焉夫天下之人其墨而毦
酷而不檢者亡論已至如勃勃巉巉號爲
punctuated:
又枝蔓其細瑣而蔽之，孰與寧棄功而免患？無惑乎宵人負靑而營窟，局士信節以守株。盲者處暗而譚離婁之明，躄者端坐而矜許少之捷；貌羊質以虎皮，飾鴞鳴以鳳釆。本體愈不可識，而沉痼益以眩人，上下相貿，豪傑何由而顯乎？所謂「草昧之初恒多賢，熈洽之後常乏才」者，語不誣也。
明興，列聖重光，治化汪濊。我皇上以冲睿繼統，用人行政，鋭意興修二祖之軌；頊憂士習稍媮，治理踳駁，特申禁令，飭學校，嚴評汰，復久任。精覈之政，瑩然烈於往古。而疆圉介冑，能秉障破敵、抵掌籌邊，旋起徒步、建大將。一時德意所敷，薄海風靡，文武吏士莫不盱衡而肩當世之務，投筆而修羽檄之功，豈患乏才哉？
第愚竊有異焉。夫天下之人，其墨而毦、酷而不檢者，亡論已；至如勃勃巉巉，號爲
translation_en:
… others will spin out tangled objections over trivialities to obscure them—is it not better to renounce such achievements and escape calamity? No wonder, then, that petty men carry filth on their backs while burrowing out their dens [?], and narrow-minded scholars cling to rigid conventions as if waiting by a tree stump for a hare. The blind sit in darkness and talk of the keen sight of Li Lou; the lame sit upright and boast of the agility of Xu Shao [?]; the substance of a sheep is disguised in a tiger's skin, and the screech of an owl is decked out in the plumage of a phoenix. As true substance becomes ever harder to discern, deep-seated maladies increasingly dazzle and confuse people. When superiors and inferiors thus deceive and trade upon one another, how can heroic men of talent ever come to prominence? The saying that "at the rugged dawn of a dynasty worthy men are always abundant, whereas in an era of peaceful prosperity talent is often lacking" is by no means unfounded.

Since the rise of the Ming, successive sage emperors have added radiance to one another, and their transformative governance has been vast and deep. Our reigning Sovereign, having succeeded to the throne in youthful wisdom, employs men and conducts administration with a keen determination to revive and cultivate the standards of the Two Ancestors (Taizu and Chengzu). Anxiously concerned that the habits of the literati have grown somewhat lax and that governance has become contradictory and confused, He has specially reiterated prohibitions and ordinances, rectified the schools, tightened evaluations and eliminations, and restored long tenures of office. His policy of rigorous verification shines more illustriously than that of antiquity. Moreover, among the armored warriors on the frontiers, those capable of holding the ramparts, smashing the enemy, and clapping their hands while devising border strategies are swiftly raised from the ranks of common foot soldiers and established as grand generals. Wherever His virtuous intentions are spread at this time, all within the seas are swept along as by the wind; civil and military officials and officers alike all raise their brows to shoulder the affairs of the age, or cast aside the writing brush to cultivate the merits of feathered war-dispatches. How could there be any worry over a lack of talent?

Yet in my humble opinion, I privately view the matter somewhat differently. Among the people of the empire, those who are greedy and dull [?], or harsh and unrestrained, need not even be discussed. As for those who are spirited and towering, acclaimed as…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
有材者百一耳而材之中又超逸絕倫號
爲豪傑者萬一耳豪傑不數見而中村比
比也顧欲進中材而上之非法莫由矣請
以馬喻夫馬之有騏驥亦猶豪傑之於人
至寥鮮也使庸人御之卽騏驥亦困不前
已惟王良則整齊其銜勒而調適其步趨
雖駑劣下乘將不化而騏驥哉當其驥而
困也尾湛胅潰負棘悲號抑何鈍也及其
駑而化也行安性得一息千里又何捷也
===
此無他蓋良能正法以馳驟之而他人不
然耳繇斯以談馭中材之法惡容以無講
乎是故度才德之品究聲華之實削身格
之限塞告訐之門行激勸之典此五者法
之所貴也何以明之夫湛盧不可以刈禾
犀象不可以秉耜言殊用也今程事者兼
數職於一人任鴻鉅於委瑣譬之負蚉以
山試蛙以轍也受之者不自量是拳而舂
黍躄而踰嶮也均失其當矣誠能錄長棄
punctuated: 有材者，百一耳；而材之中，又超逸絕倫、號爲豪傑者，萬一耳。豪傑不數見，而中村比比也。顧欲進中材而上之，非法莫由矣。請以馬喻：夫馬之有騏驥，亦猶豪傑之於人，至寥鮮也。使庸人御之，卽騏驥亦困不前已；惟王良則整齊其銜勒，而調適其步趨，雖駑劣下乘，將不化而騏驥哉？當其驥而困也，尾湛胅潰，負棘悲號，抑何鈍也！及其駑而化也，行安性得，一息千里，又何捷也！此無他，蓋良能正法以馳驟之，而他人不然耳。繇斯以談，馭中材之法，惡容以無講乎？是故度才德之品，究聲華之實，削身格之限，塞告訐之門，行激勸之典，此五者，法之所貴也。何以明之？夫湛盧不可以刈禾，犀象不可以秉耜，言殊用也。今程事者，兼數職於一人，任鴻鉅於委瑣，譬之負蚉以山，試蛙以轍也；受之者不自量，是拳而舂黍，躄而踰嶮也。均失其當矣。誠能錄長棄
translation_en: …possessed of talent are scarcely one in a hundred; and among the talented, those who are transcendent and peerless, styled heroic exemplars, are scarcely one in ten thousand. Heroic exemplars are rarely seen, whereas people of middling talent are everywhere. Yet if one wishes to advance those of middling talent and elevate them, there is no way to do so except through proper method. Allow me to illustrate this with horses: among horses, fine steeds like Qiji are just like heroic exemplars among men—extremely rare and few. If an ordinary person drives them, even a Qiji will become exhausted and fail to advance. Only Wang Liang adjusts their bits and reins in order and harmonizes their pace and stride; then even an inferior, worn-out nag—will it not be transformed into a Qiji? When a fine steed is exhausted, its tail is soaked and its flanks are ruptured [?], bearing thorns and crying out in sorrow—how sluggish it is! Yet when a nag is transformed, its gait is steady and its nature is satisfied, covering a thousand li in a single breath—how swift it is! This is for no other reason than that Wang Liang was able to gallop them according to the correct method, whereas others were not. Speaking from this perspective, how can we afford not to examine the method of managing those of middling talent? Therefore, measuring the grade of talent and virtue, investigating the reality behind reputation and splendor, removing the restrictions of status and qualification, blocking the gate of malicious accusations, and carrying out the statutes of encouragement and exhortation—these five are what proper method values. How can this be made clear? The sword Zhanlu cannot be used to reap grain, nor can rhinoceroses and elephants be used to hold a plowshare; this means their uses are different. Nowadays, those who assign tasks combine several offices in a single person, or entrust great and weighty matters to petty and trivial men; this is like making a mosquito carry a mountain on its back, or testing a frog in a carriage rut. Those who accept such tasks without taking their own measure are like someone with curled-up hands pounding millet, or someone lame in both legs crossing a precipitous pass. Both miss what is appropriate. If one can truly record strengths and discard…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
短取瑜掩瑕河渠之使不責以米鹽法比
之家不勞以兵革則人必爭襮其所能而
無隱賢蔽善之失此才德之品所宜度也
驪牛之黃犅虎幽莠之生類穀似惑之也
夫人才亦猶是耳今目蕩檢爲恢弘虛憍
爲豪傑詞營爲高明騷屑爲果敢將何以
經方致遠甄物成化乎誠能敦純慤則要
軼歛容重沉潛則銜霍順首卽凡哆經綸
於脣吻迷本眞於面目者亦皆攄忱畢愫
而不忍欺矣此聲華之實所宜究也蛟龍
獲制於螻螘鯨鰲取困於牛涔限於地也
===
兹
國家所選士自三途外故無增耳假令魁人
喆士一屈於詞場則終身不齒於縉紳故
博士以頹齡喪守而持劵規財黠世弗恤
矣掾史以下局摧心而舞文府利渨淩足
羞矣不知古有皓首而爲帝師以文無害
而登閣相業左驗甚明也而可拘譾以域
punctuated: 短，取瑜掩瑕，河渠之使不責以米鹽，法比之家不勞以兵革，則人必爭襮其所能，而無隱賢蔽善之失。此才德之品所宜度也。驪牛之黃犅虎，幽莠之生類穀，似惑之也。夫人才亦猶是耳。今目蕩檢爲恢弘，虛憍爲豪傑，詞營爲高明，騷屑爲果敢，將何以經方致遠，甄物成化乎？誠能敦純慤，則要軼歛容；重沉潛，則銜霍順首；卽凡哆經綸於脣吻，迷本眞於面目者，亦皆攄忱畢愫而不忍欺矣。此聲華之實所宜究也。蛟龍獲制於螻螘，鯨鰲取困於牛涔，限於地也。兹國家所選士，自三途外，故無增耳。假令魁人喆士，一屈於詞場，則終身不齒於縉紳。故博士以頹齡喪守，而持劵規財，黠世弗恤矣；掾史以下局摧心，而舞文府利，渨淩足羞矣。不知古有皓首而爲帝師，以文無害而登閣，相業左驗甚明也，而可拘譾以域
translation_en:
…their shortcomings, taking their fine qualities while overlooking their flaws—not holding commissioners of waterways responsible for grain and salt accounts, nor burdening specialists in legal precedents with military campaigns—then men will surely vie to display their abilities, and there will be no error of obscuring the worthy and eclipsing the good. This is why the grades of talent and virtue ought to be measured.

A brindled ox may look like a yellow-striped tiger [?], and growing weeds resemble grain; it is the resemblance that confuses people. Human talent is just like this. Today, if we regard the flouting of restraint as magnanimity, empty arrogance as heroism, verbal scheming as lofty brilliance, and restless agitation as decisiveness, how then shall we order the realm, reach distant goals, discern things, and complete transformative rule? If we can truly esteem pure sincerity, the unruly and reckless will compose their countenances; if we value calm depth, the ostentatious and flamboyant [?] will bow their heads in submission. Even all those who boast of statecraft with their lips while masking their true nature in their faces will pour out their genuine feelings and utmost sincerity, not bearing to deceive. This is why the reality behind reputation and outward splendor ought to be investigated.

Flood-dragons come under the control of mole-crickets and ants, and whales and giant sea-turtles find themselves trapped in a hoof-print puddle, because they are restricted by their environment. Now, in the Dynasty's selection of scholars, outside of the three regular paths of entry, nothing further has been added. Suppose an outstanding man or wise scholar suffers a single setback in the examination grounds; for the rest of his life he is not ranked as an equal among the gentry officials. Thus erudites, losing their integrity in declining years, clutch tallies to scheme for wealth, showing no concern for a cunning world; subofficial functionaries, their spirits crushed in lowly posts, manipulate the wording of the statutes to hoard profit, their sordidness and abusiveness truly shameful. People fail to realize that in antiquity there were those who became Imperial Tutors with hoary heads, and those who ascended to the Grand Secretariat on the strength of impeccable legal clerical work—the corroborating evidence of their achievements as chief councilors is crystal clear. How then can we cling to narrow views and fence in…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
才乎此身格之限所宜削也語云衆喣漂
山叢輕折軸見物偏積則勢自移所以喻
讒也故夫市之無虎井之無人非孺子所
明邪蠚然倡之輒閧然信之往往因形吠
聲以一成百不至於改易睹聽不止今譎
佞者以養交獵譽則其實必浮樸茂者以
忤俗招尤則其毀必誕此朝跖暮夷貝錦
易侈甲清乙濁蒼蠅易汙而隻字之紙一
夫之頰顧安足以爲據乎此告訐之門所
===
宜塞也傳有之有功不賞有罪不罰雖唐
虞不能以化天下何者令之所驅固民之
所向也是故越淵谷者奔千金之利則先
趨畏猛虎之逼則後至閭里素封藿肉布
緆役貧挾窘則厮輿爲之用烏合白徒怒
齦膹目喑嗚咄嗟則草澤爲之傾矧操黜
陟之柄握生殺之權者乎誠能懸不測之
賞使天下有所跂焉而時動其慷慨奮厲
之懷施不測之罰使天下有所懾焉而陰
punctuated: 才乎？此身格之限所宜削也。語云：「衆喣漂山，叢輕折軸。」見物偏積，則勢自移，所以喻讒也。故夫市之無虎、井之無人，非孺子所明邪？蠚然倡之，輒閧然信之，往往因形吠聲，以一成百，不至於改易睹聽不止。今譎佞者以養交獵譽，則其實必浮；樸茂者以忤俗招尤，則其毀必誕。此朝跖暮夷，貝錦易侈；甲清乙濁，蒼蠅易汙。而隻字之紙、一夫之頰，顧安足以爲據乎？此告訐之門所宜塞也。傳有之：「有功不賞，有罪不罰，雖唐、虞不能以化天下。」何者？令之所驅，固民之所向也。是故越淵谷者，奔千金之利則先趨，畏猛虎之逼則後至。閭里素封，藿肉布緆，役貧挾窘，則厮輿爲之用；烏合白徒，怒齦膹目，喑嗚咄嗟，則草澤爲之傾。矧操黜陟之柄、握生殺之權者乎？誠能懸不測之賞，使天下有所跂焉，而時動其慷慨奮厲之懷；施不測之罰，使天下有所懾焉，而陰…
translation_en:
…restrict talent? This is why the limitations of status and qualification ought to be pared away.

The proverb says: "Many breaths can float a mountain; heaped-up trifles can break an axle." This shows that when things accumulate on one side, the balance of power naturally shifts—a metaphor for slander. Now, that there is no tiger in the marketplace and no man in the well—is this not obvious even to a child? Yet when someone starts a stinging rumor, people immediately believe it in an uproar; time and again they bark at shadows and echo sounds, turning one thing into a hundred, never stopping until they have confounded what people see and hear. Today, the deceitful and flattering cultivate connections to hunt for fame, so their reputation is bound to exceed reality; the simple and upright offend vulgar custom and invite blame, so the slanders against them are bound to be preposterous. Thus a Robber Zhi in the morning becomes a Boyi by evening, as shell-brocade patterns of calumny are easily embellished; when one man is pure and another muddy, green flies easily sully the clean. How, then, can a scrap of paper with a few words or the tongue of a single man be sufficient as evidence? This is why the gate of denunciations and accusations ought to be blocked.

Tradition has it: "If merit is not rewarded and crime is not punished, even Tang Yao and Yu Shun could not transform the world." Why is this? Because what orders drive forward is naturally what the people turn toward. Therefore, among those crossing abysses and valleys, those chasing a profit of a thousand pieces of gold will rush ahead first, while those fearing the press of a fierce tiger will arrive last. When anuntitled rich man of the alleys, with his bean-leaf fare and coarse cloth, employs the poor and takes advantage of the hard-pressed, menials and grooms will serve him; when a mob of unattached commoners bares its gums in rage and glares with bulging eyes, bellowing and barking commands, the marshes and wilds are swayed by them. How much more so for one who holds the handle of demotion and promotion and grasps the power of life and death! If one can truly hold out unfathomable rewards, making the world stand on tiptoe in expectation and constantly stirring its generous and spirited resolve, and mete out unfathomable punishments, making the world stand in awe and secretly…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
耗其私邪儌嚚之氣庶被賞者愈砥節首
公悉謀力以自効而蒙罰者益懲尤寡悔
競濯磨以自新矣此激勸之典所宜行也
夫五法舉則中材質行在上者皆銓別而
器使之得以揚著所長補重
國家起沮傷之風振偈𢡟之吏是馭才之要
機而興賢之至術也又安有挾僻飾文試
身冒法甘底弗類而不化爲豪傑者乎愚
往聞
皇上臨御之初嘗大計來
朝之吏而
拔其治效異等者
召見於
庭
寵錫勞勉逮貪暴之尤者以法斯所謂不測之
賞罰也即今文武諸臣及以事展
覲者或紹舉玆典時一
召問別其材品
punctuated:
耗其私邪儌嚚之氣，庶被賞者愈砥節首公，悉謀力以自効，而蒙罰者益懲尤寡悔，競濯磨以自新矣。此激勸之典所宜行也。
夫五法舉，則中材質行，在上者皆銓別而器使之，得以揚著所長，補重國家，起沮傷之風，振偈𢡟之吏，是馭才之要機，而興賢之至術也。又安有挾僻飾文，試身冒法，甘底弗類，而不化爲豪傑者乎？愚往聞皇上臨御之初，嘗大計來朝之吏，而拔其治效異等者，召見於庭，寵錫勞勉；逮貪暴之尤者以法。斯所謂不測之賞罰也。即今文武諸臣及以事展覲者，或紹舉玆典，時一召問，別其材品，
translation_en:
…diminish their selfish, perverse, opportunistic, and deceitful spirit, then perhaps those who receive rewards will all the more whet their integrity and put the public good first, exhausting their counsels and strength to render service, while those who suffer punishment will increasingly take warning from their faults to minimize regrets, competing to cleanse and polish themselves in self-renewal. This is why the statutes for rousing and encouraging officials ought to be put into practice.

Now, when these five methods are instituted, then as for those of average talent and substantive conduct, their superiors will evaluate, distinguish, and employ them according to their capacities, enabling them to display and manifest their strengths, bring added weight to the state, revive demoralized customs, and rouse sluggish and negligent [?] officials. This is the essential mechanism for managing talent and the ultimate art of promoting the worthy. How then could there still be anyone who harbors perversity and embellishes himself with empty Artifice, testing his person by defying the law and willingly sinking into unworthiness, rather than transforming into a person of outstanding caliber?

I, in my ignorance, have heard that in the past, at the beginning of His Majesty's reign, during the Great Reckoning of officials who came to court for audience, He selected those whose administrative results were of exceptional grade, summoned them to an audience in the palace courtyard, and graciously bestowed gifts and words of encouragement upon them; while He arrested the most egregious of the corrupt and tyrannical and subjected them to the law. This is what is meant by unfathomable rewards and punishments. If today, with the various civil and military officials as well as those coming to court on official business for an audience, He were perhaps to resume and carry out this institutional practice, occasionally summoning and questioning them to distinguish their talents and character, …

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
雷霆雨露人豈能測乎蓋五法之中此爲至要
愚生所惓惓引領者也雖然此直論於法
之內耳若夫豪傑殆無法而勸者也彼不
事吾法而吾法之與中材等此不羈之士
所以扼腕憤胸掉臂解體而終不顧於世
也有由然矣是故士誠豪傑已任誠有所
必專已即如謗書盈篋弗視不爲縱捐金
恣所出弗問不爲疎如武之不罪矯制而
不謂之失紀宣之不阻留田而不謂之老
===
師要以披肝膈釋嫌隙恢文罔假便宜而
不以區區之法縛束其所爲誠優之也任
豪傑不當如是邪噫法內法也法之外而
能鼓舞豪傑亦法也蓋法之內固與法之
外交相資焉耳天下豈有廢法而登諸理
者哉此又用豪傑者不可不察也
第四問
潘大復
同考試官訓導王　批〔東南重地民困未蘇非細故也〕
punctuated:
雷霆雨露，人豈能測乎？蓋五法之中，此爲至要，愚生所惓惓引領者也。雖然，此直論於法之內耳；若夫豪傑，殆無法而勸者也。彼不事吾法，而吾法之，與中材等，此不羈之士所以扼腕憤胸、掉臂解體，而終不顧於世也，有由然矣。是故士誠豪傑已，任誠有所必專已，即如謗書盈篋，弗視不爲縱；捐金恣所出，弗問不爲疎。如武之不罪矯制，而不謂之失紀；宣之不阻留田，而不謂之老師。要以披肝膈、釋嫌隙、恢文罔、假便宜，而不以區區之法縛束其所爲，誠優之也。任豪傑不當如是邪？噫！法內，法也；法之外而能鼓舞豪傑，亦法也。蓋法之內固與法之外交相資焉耳。天下豈有廢法而登諸理者哉？此又用豪傑者不可不察也。
第四問
潘大復
同考試官訓導王　批〔東南重地，民困未蘇，非細故也。〕
translation_en:
… thunderbolts and rain and dew, how could anyone fathom them? Indeed, among the five methods, this is the most essential, and what this foolish student earnestly cranes his neck hoping to see. Even so, this only discusses what lies within the law. As for heroic men of talent, they are practically those who take encouragement without need of laws. They do not occupy themselves with our laws, yet if we subject them to the law on a par with men of mediocre talent, that is why untrammeled scholars wring their wrists with indignation in their breasts, swing their arms and lose heart, and in the end turn their backs on the world—there is a reason for it! Therefore, once a scholar is truly a man of heroic talent, and his commission is truly one that must be granted exclusive authority, then even if slanderous letters fill a chest, not looking at them is not indulgence [alluding to Marquis Wen of Wei and Yue Yang]; and if funds are bestowed for him to spend as he pleases, not auditing them is not negligence [alluding to Liu Bang and Chen Ping]. Thus Emperor Wu of Han did not punish forging a decree, yet it was not called a breach of discipline [alluding to Ji An]; Emperor Xuan of Han did not block the proposal to remain and farm the frontier, yet it was not called wearing out the army [alluding to Zhao Chongguo]. In short, by baring one's heart and innermost thoughts, dispelling suspicions and rifts, relaxing the meshes of the legal code, and granting discretionary authority, rather than binding their actions with petty regulations, one truly treats them with generous distinction. Should not employing heroic men of talent be like this? Alas! What is within the law is law; being able to inspire and rouse heroic men of talent outside the law is also law. For what lies within the law and what lies outside the law surely complement and aid one another. How could the empire ever abolish the law and yet ascend to good governance? This, too, is what he who employs heroic men of talent cannot fail to examine.

Fourth Question

Pan Dafu 潘大復

Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Wang: 〔The southeast is a region of vital importance, and the people's distress has not yet been relieved—this is no trivial matter. …〕

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
是作究極病源及所爲佐元元之急者可稱切中是有用之學也宜錄
之
考試官修撰沈　批〔書生言閭里事卽涉迂濶然意獨在生民耳草茅之語可以佐治殆謂是耶〕
考試官左賛善沈　批〔說東南民瘼及所以寛恤之政析如指掌似嘗抱先憂之志者是以錄之〕
執事惘然念東南民力策所振救之方諸
生念此至熟也卽不問顧有所關說且東
南之事非難明也民之疾苦至可憂也肯
一加心易爲力也紘急者乖號悲者嘎執
事略其狂試垂聽焉蓋審於天下之勢可
以知畏矣明於治世之道可以廣德矣持
之磐石揺之累碁萬世不爲久一旦不爲
驟是天下之勢也安可不知畏望腹而易
其饑挾纊而易其寒衽席而易其危引考
而易其札瘥夭厲是治世之道也安可不
廣德知畏先於結人心人心悅天下之勢
固矣廣德先於恤窮民窮民遂治世之道
punctuated:
是作究極病源，及所爲佐元元之急者，可稱切中，是有用之學也，宜錄之。〕
考試官修撰沈　批：〔書生言閭里事，卽涉迂濶，然意獨在生民耳。草茅之語，可以佐治，殆謂是耶？〕
考試官左賛善沈　批：〔說東南民瘼，及所以寛恤之政，析如指掌，似嘗抱先憂之志者，是以錄之。〕

執事惘然念東南民力，策所振救之方，諸生念此至熟也，卽不問，顧有所關說。且東南之事，非難明也；民之疾苦，至可憂也；肯一加心，易爲力也。紘急者乖，號悲者嘎，執事略其狂，試垂聽焉。蓋審於天下之勢，可以知畏矣；明於治世之道，可以廣德矣。持之磐石，揺之累碁，萬世不爲久，一旦不爲驟，是天下之勢也，安可不知畏？望腹而易其饑，挾纊而易其寒，衽席而易其危，引考而易其札瘥夭厲，是治世之道也，安可不廣德？知畏先於結人心，人心悅，天下之勢固矣；廣德先於恤窮民，窮民遂，治世之道…
translation_en:
… This essay thoroughly investigates the root of the malady, and what it proposes to relieve the urgent distress of the common people can be called right on the mark. This is practical learning; it ought to be selected for inclusion.]
Examiner and Senior Compiler Shen comments: [When a scholar speaks of village affairs, even if he strays into impracticality, his concern lies solely with the livelihood of the people. "The words of the unranked rustic can assist in governance"—does that not refer to just such a work as this?]
Examiner and Left Admonisher Shen comments: [In discussing the hardships of the people in the Southeast and the policies for lenient relief, he analyzes them as clearly as pointing to one's own palm. He seems to be one who has long cherished the ambition of "worrying before the world worries," and therefore we select his essay for inclusion.]

Your Excellency, with deep concern, ponders the exhausted strength of the people in the Southeast and asks in this policy question for ways to rescue and revive them. I, a student, have reflected upon this most thoroughly; even had you not asked, I would still have wished to speak on the matter. Moreover, the affairs of the Southeast are not difficult to understand; the sufferings of the people are cause for the utmost anxiety; yet if one is willing to apply one's heart to it even once, it is easy to take effective action. When a string is stretched too taut, it snaps out of tune; when one cries out in grief too long, the voice grows hoarse. May Your Excellency overlook my rashness and deign to listen.

Indeed, by examining the strategic condition of the Empire, one learns what to fear; by understanding the Way of governing the world, one can broaden imperial virtue. Upheld, the realm is as stable as a great boulder; shaken, it is as precarious as stacked chessmen. Ten thousand generations is not too long for it to endure, yet a single morning is not too sudden for it to collapse—such is the strategic condition of the Empire. How can one not know fear? Giving the people full bellies in place of their hunger, wrapping them in floss silk in place of their cold, placing them upon secure mats in place of their peril, and guiding them to longevity in place of pestilence, disease, and premature death—such is the Way of governing the world. How can one not broaden virtue? Knowing fear begins with binding the hearts of the people; when the hearts of the people are pleased, the strategic condition of the Empire is secure. Broadening virtue begins with showing compassion to the destitute; when the destitute are able to thrive, the Way of governing the world…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
得矣執道以極世先勢而底寧明君之畫
也何可不察焉
國家財賦仰給東南我
太祖當創業之初經費甚繁所爲愛養休息民
力者無不加之意愼擇長吏嚴察不才以
時逐去尤重欺蔽不卹民之罰蠲除之
詔間歲一下或竝蠲或蠲其半或減重額尤加
意于東南諸郡蓋在位三十餘載而東南
被蠲除厚渥者幾二十
===
詔焉豈不念財賦之數而令民徼恩澤哉蓋寡
取於民撙節用之自可不詘念民力一竭
不可復振力竭不振則無以爲生無以爲
生則不能給公家有無聊之心急之易動
煽之易搖故不若寬之使有餘此
遠猷遡慮繫人心而垂不拔之基者也我
皇上紹熙洽之業寰宇殷富淸和咸理東南之
民乃日以困比歲災傷室若懸磬鬻妻棄
稚有不得顧取木皮野蕪以爲糧甚或羣
punctuated:
得矣。執道以極世，先勢而底寧，明君之畫也，何可不察焉？
國家財賦仰給東南。我太祖當創業之初，經費甚繁，所爲愛養休息民力者，無不加之意。愼擇長吏，嚴察不才，以時逐去，尤重欺蔽不卹民之罰。蠲除之詔，間歲一下，或竝蠲，或蠲其半，或減重額，尤加意于東南諸郡。蓋在位三十餘載，而東南被蠲除厚渥者，幾二十詔焉。豈不念財賦之數，而令民徼恩澤哉？蓋寡取於民，撙節用之，自可不詘。念民力一竭，不可復振；力竭不振，則無以爲生；無以爲生，則不能給公家。有無聊之心，急之易動，煽之易搖，故不若寬之使有餘。此遠猷遡慮，繫人心而垂不拔之基者也。
我皇上紹熙洽之業，寰宇殷富，淸和咸理，東南之民乃日以困。比歲災傷，室若懸磬，鬻妻棄稚，有不得顧，取木皮野蕪以爲糧，甚或羣
translation_en:
… attained. Upholding the Way to bring the age to perfection and anticipating the trend of events to establish peace—this is the design of an enlightened ruler; how could one not examine it?

The fiscal revenues of the state rely upon the southeast for supply. At the beginning of the founding of the dynasty, although our Grand Progenitor (Taizu) faced极为 numerous expenditures, in all that concerned cherishing, nurturing, and giving rest to the strength of the people, there was nothing to which he did not pay special heed. He carefully selected senior local officials, strictly investigated the incompetent and dismissed them in timely fashion, and made especially heavy the punishments for deceiving the throne and failing to show compassion for the people. Edicts remitting taxes were issued every other year—sometimes remitting all, sometimes remitting half, and sometimes reducing heavy quotas—with particular attention paid to the prefectures of the southeast. Indeed, during his reign of more than thirty years, the southeast received the generous grace of tax remissions in nearly twenty edicts. Was it that he did not consider the figures of fiscal revenue and merely let the people seek unmerited bounty? Rather, if one takes little from the people and uses it with frugal restraint, resources will naturally not be exhausted. He reflected that once the people's strength is depleted, it cannot be revived; when their strength is depleted and cannot be revived, they have no means of livelihood; and when they have no means of livelihood, they cannot supply the public treasury. When they harbor a sense of hopelessness, if pressed hard they are easily driven to commotion, and if incited they are easily shaken; therefore, it is better to treat them leniently so that they have a surplus. This was his far-reaching plan and deep foresight, binding the hearts of the people and handing down an unshakeable foundation.

Our August Emperor has inherited a flourishing and harmonious enterprise; the realm is prosperous and abundant, and in clarity and harmony all is well governed, yet the people of the southeast grow more distressed by the day. In recent years, natural disasters have brought ruin, leaving homes as bare as hanging chimes. Men sell their wives and abandon their young children without being able to look back, gathering tree bark and wild weeds for food, and in extreme cases even banding together…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
哄而椎摽死亡流離相望于路所在嗷嗷
民心不寧非獨淮鳳蘇松也若是者無異
故焉惟是小大臣工不能奉宣
德意之過也先是建議者慮衆志偷縱而治隳
稍稍控名責實意非不美而有司一切持
祿位不以民爲意民既無年不能完歲課
并責其積逋追呼滿道雞犬騷然重掠治
之往往而斃愁怨之氣上干天和災眚無
時盜賊多有曾無振業之方而催徵之急
===
有加於舊彼豈不知民之糜骨不足以供
哉苟欲以明其釐條職而逃罪責耳有馬
於此使人牧之束縛鞭箠妨其齕草飲水
之性使窮而斃也豈不甚哉
皇上惻然動念行賑卹蠲積逋民欣欣有更生
之望愚生在涸轍中未敢賀無恙也東南
固若瘵尫然視其起居食飲謂恙未甚力
竭而不支久矣不能自言所苦一旦顛仆
乃知耳今所爲議賑者豈非爲民不能自
punctuated: 哄而椎摽，死亡流離，相望于路，所在嗷嗷，民心不寧，非獨淮、鳳、蘇、松也。若是者無異故焉，惟是小大臣工不能奉宣德意之過也。先是建議者慮衆志偷縱而治隳，稍稍控名責實，意非不美。而有司一切持祿位，不以民爲意。民既無年，不能完歲課，并責其積逋，追呼滿道，雞犬騷然。重掠治之，往往而斃。愁怨之氣，上干天和，災眚無時，盜賊多有。曾無振業之方，而催徵之急有加於舊。彼豈不知民之糜骨不足以供哉？苟欲以明其釐條職而逃罪責耳。有馬於此，使人牧之，束縛鞭箠，妨其齕草飲水之性，使窮而斃也，豈不甚哉？皇上惻然動念，行賑卹，蠲積逋，民欣欣有更生之望。愚生在涸轍中，未敢賀無恙也。東南固若瘵尫然，視其起居食飲，謂恙未甚，力竭而不支久矣，不能自言所苦，一旦顛仆乃知耳。今所爲議賑者，豈非爲民不能自
translation_en:
…clamor in mobs and plunder by force. The dead and the displaced are within sight of one another along the roads; everywhere there are cries of distress, and the people's hearts are restless—not only in Huai'an, Fengyang, Suzhou, and Songjiang. That things have come to such a pass has no other cause than the fault of officials great and small failing to uphold and propagate the Emperor's benevolent intentions.

Earlier, those who offered counsel, worrying that public morale had grown lax and indulgent and that governance was deteriorating, gradually sought to hold performance accountable to title. Their intention was by no means unadmirable. Yet the local authorities are entirely bent on preserving their emoluments and posts, giving no thought to the people. When the people suffer a year of crop failure and cannot complete their annual tax quota, the authorities simultaneously demand payment of their accumulated arrears. Tax collectors' shouts fill the roads, throwing even the chickens and dogs into an uproar. The people are subjected to severe flogging and punishment, and frequently die from it. The aura of grief and resentment rises to offend heavenly harmony; natural disasters occur at all seasons, and bandits and thieves abound. Yet there is no plan at all to relieve and restore their livelihoods, while the urgency of tax collection grows even more pressing than before. How could those officials not know that even grinding the people's bones to dust would not suffice to meet the demands? They merely wish to demonstrate that they arePutting their itemized duties in order [?] so as to escape blame and punishment. Suppose there is a horse here, and one has a man tend it: if he ties it up and whips it, interfering with its natural need to graze on grass and drink water until it isdriven to exhaustion and dies, is that notgoing too far?

His Majesty, moved with compassion, has carried out relief and aid and remitted accumulated arrears, so that the people joyfully cherish the hope of a new lease on life. Yet this foolish student, like a fish in a dry rut, dares not yet offer congratulations that all is well. The Southeast is indeed like a consumptive and emaciated cripple: looking at his daily movements, food, and drink, one might say his illness is not yet extreme, though his strength has long been exhausted and unsustainable; he cannot voice his own suffering, and only when he suddenly collapses is it recognized. Now, as for the current deliberations on providing relief, is it not because the people cannot feed themselves…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
食而食之自食且不能曷能出賦稅他日
之積逋方未已也歲積一歲有司能不併
督如前時乎即幸赦之民已困矣所傷多
矣竊觀
訓律所載但被災之處所司早爲報
聞勘蠲本年之糧稅不聞其必積逋也何則其
時之爲有司者度民不能辦即爲請免不
俟爲積逋也有不爲民請者誅罰且隨之
不至民窮且恐也今日急務意者亦望仰
===
聖祖自今以後或於被災特甚之地儻
法
垂膏澤即量蠲本年歲額之輸令煢煢赤子
沾恩速而得生近方之賑濟蠲逋功實百
焉何者待饑而與之食食且不周不若與
之令自食也待積逋而除之民且甚困不
若令逋不積也千金之子忼慨喜施猶能
出餘積匡救困煢折券棄責以收人心發
名譽況以配地之富言脫口而仁恩翔者
punctuated: 食而食之？自食且不能，曷能出賦稅？他日之積逋方未已也。歲積一歲，有司能不併督如前時乎？即幸赦之，民已困矣，所傷多矣。竊觀訓律所載，但被災之處，所司早爲報聞，勘蠲本年之糧稅，不聞其必積逋也。何則？其時之爲有司者，度民不能辦，即爲請免，不俟爲積逋也；有不爲民請者，誅罰且隨之，不至民窮且恐也。今日急務，意者亦望仰聖祖，自今以後，或於被災特甚之地，儻法垂膏澤，即量蠲本年歲額之輸，令煢煢赤子沾恩速而得生近，方之賑濟蠲逋，功實百焉。何者？待饑而與之食，食且不周，不若與之令自食也；待積逋而除之，民且甚困，不若令逋不積也。千金之子，忼慨喜施，猶能出餘積匡救困煢，折券棄責，以收人心，發名譽；況以配地之富，言脫口而仁恩翔者
translation_en:
…feed themselves, and thus feeding them? If they cannot even feed themselves, how can they pay taxes? In the days to come, the accumulated arrears will still not cease. As one year's arrears pile upon another's, how can the authorities avoid pressing for combined collection just as before? Even if they are fortunate enough to have them remitted, the people are already exhausted and the damage done is already great.

I have privately observed what is recorded in the Ancestral Injunctions and the Great Ming Code: whenever a place suffers a disaster, the responsible authorities are to report it early to the throne, investigate, and remit the grain taxes for that current year; one does not hear that they must become accumulated arrears. Why is this? Because those who served as officials at that time, judging that the people could not manage to pay, immediately requested an exemption for them, without waiting for the taxes to become accumulated arrears. If anyone failed to petition on behalf of the people, punishment and penalties followed upon them, so it never came to the point where the people were driven to exhaustion and fear.

As for the urgent task of today, perhaps one may hope to look up to and emulate the Sacred Ancestor [Note: the line order here has 法 on the next column after 聖祖…之地儻, i.e., 仰法聖祖]. From now on, if in places particularly hard hit by disaster, the Emperor would perchance bestow the fertilizing dew of his grace and proportionally remit the delivery of the current year's annual quota, allowing the solitary and helpless common folk to receive grace swiftly and find a livelihood close at hand—compared to providing famine relief and remitting accumulated arrears, the merit would truly be a hundredfold! Why is this? Waiting until they are starving to give them food—and the food not even reaching everyone—is not as good as giving them the means to feed themselves; waiting until arrears have accumulated to cancel them—by which time the people are already sorely distressed—is not as good as preventing the arrears from accumulating in the first place. The son of a family worth a thousand pieces of gold, generous and fond of charity, is still able to bring out his surplus savings to rescue the distressed and solitary, breaking tally-deeds and cancelling debts in order to win people's hearts and spread his good name; how much more so for One who possesses wealth matching the earth, from whose lips a single word spoken sends benevolent grace soaring…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
乎此所謂肯一加心易爲力也說者必曰
恐黠桀之衆故逋而徼恩嗟乎上以誠心
愛民未有不以誠心應者年穀順成而逋
賦彼將何執爲生見
上甚畏天閔民而有司者無能憂民所苦先時
以請遂使
德惠不宣民不蒙澤比覩
詔旨已曉然洞燭之矣夫蠲與賑豈不減公儲
哉特與之後時惠雖渥民不飽所以妄謂
===
東南之瘵今未愈者此也雖然微獨此矣
語有之峻嶺無嵗蓺之木駛流無掉尾之
鱗政煩無逸樂之民故足溫而心平人佚
而國寧刑罰者民之寒暑也不可不適也
敎令者民之風雨也不可不節也蓼莪成
行簡絲數米可以治三畝之宫非治天下
之體也聖王臨下以簡平易近民非簡不
可以治大非易不可以合衆易故能天簡
故能地宜其爲天下往也生觀前代能休
punctuated: 乎？此所謂肯一加心，易爲力也。說者必曰：「恐黠桀之衆，故逋而徼恩。」嗟乎！上以誠心愛民，未有不以誠心應者。年穀順成而逋賦，彼將何執爲？生見上甚畏天閔民，而有司者無能憂民所苦，先時以請，遂使德惠不宣，民不蒙澤。比覩詔旨，已曉然洞燭之矣。夫蠲與賑豈不減公儲哉？特與之後時，惠雖渥，民不飽，所以妄謂東南之瘵今未愈者，此也。雖然，微獨此矣。語有之：「峻嶺無嵗蓺之木，駛流無掉尾之鱗，政煩無逸樂之民。」故足溫而心平，人佚而國寧。刑罰者，民之寒暑也，不可不適也；敎令者，民之風雨也，不可不節也。蓼莪成行，簡絲數米，可以治三畝之宫，非治天下之體也。聖王臨下以簡，平易近民。非簡不可以治大，非易不可以合衆。易故能天，簡故能地，宜其爲天下往也。生觀前代能休
translation_en:
…? This is what is meant by saying that if one is only willing to apply one's heart, it is easy to accomplish. Yet commentators will surely say: "We fear that crafty and unruly people will deliberately fall into arrears in order to angle for imperial grace." Alas! When the ruler loves the people with a sincere heart, there are none who do not respond with a sincere heart. If the yearly harvests are favorable and abundant and yet they evade their taxes, what excuse could they possibly hold onto? As a student, I see that His Majesty deeply reveres Heaven and pities the people, whereas the authorities in charge are incapable of worrying over the people's sufferings and petitioning ahead of time; as a result, the imperial virtue and kindness are not promulgated, and the people do not receive the benefit of his grace. Recently, upon reading the imperial decrees, I saw that His Majesty has already clearly and thoroughly perceived this. Now, do not remissions and famine relief diminish the public reserves? It is only that when they are granted after the proper time, even though the bounty is generous, the people are not fed to fullness. The reason I presumptuously say that the affliction of the Southeast has still not been healed today is precisely this.

Even so, it is not this alone. There is a saying: "On precipitous ridges there are no trees planted year after year [?]; in swift currents there are no fish leisurely wagging their tails; under burdensome governance there are no people enjoying ease and pleasure." Therefore, when the feet are warm, the mind is calm; when the people are at ease, the state is tranquil. Punishments and penalties are the cold and heat of the people: they must be kept moderate. Instructions and ordinances are the wind and rain of the people: they must be regulated. Planting thickets of smartweed and wormwood in neat rows, sorting threads of silk, and counting grains of rice—by such means one may manage a homestead of three mu, but this is not the proper way to govern the empire. The sage kings approached their subjects with simplicity, and drew near to the people through levelness and ease. Without simplicity one cannot govern what is great; without ease one cannot unite the multitude. Because of ease, one can match Heaven; because of simplicity, one can match Earth—fitting indeed that the whole empire turns to them! As a student, when I observe those in former dynasties who were able to give rest and…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
養其民者漢稱文景唐稱太宗宋稱眞仁
寧獨躬儉德哉上意在養民不必盡行法
法以安民耳法不宜民寧使法漏毋因困
民故其時多奬用寬和木訥之吏斥遠刻
深操切之人吏固阿保也阿保非其人不
誠心以求多防奚以爲哉今者有司奉法
不如令譴責立有之民卽不堪吏且博榮
聲赫赫目前以去誰爲民言者政令所出
自部院撫按司道而下之有司止矣有司
===
何以應上哉上流急者下流決至於民而
上之所約束峻急一切受之無可言矣東
南財賦地政令特煩且先苛擾百出民曾
不得寧處托足焉卽如積穀備荒美意也
計令嚴必及數妄加銖罰以充之是積穀
病民也捕盜安民美意也計令嚴在必獲
踪跡無辜者名之以謾上是捕盜又病民
也丈田清額美意也計額盈者率得褒與
妄益名田以應令是丈田又病民也鍰贖
banxin: 乙卯鄉試錄文　百二
punctuated: 養其民者，漢稱文、景，唐稱太宗，宋稱眞、仁，寧獨躬儉德哉？上意在養民，不必盡行法。法以安民耳，法不宜民，寧使法漏，毋因困民。故其時多奬用寬和木訥之吏，斥遠刻深操切之人。吏固阿保也，阿保非其人，不誠心以求，多防奚以爲哉？今者有司奉法不如令，譴責立有之；民卽不堪，吏且博榮聲赫赫目前以去，誰爲民言者？政令所出，自部、院、撫、按、司、道，而下之有司止矣。有司何以應上哉？上流急者下流決，至於民而上之所約束峻急，一切受之，無可言矣。東南財賦地，政令特煩且先，苛擾百出，民曾不得寧處托足焉。卽如積穀備荒，美意也；計令嚴必及數，妄加銖罰以充之，是積穀病民也。捕盜安民，美意也；計令嚴在必獲，踪跡無辜者名之以謾上，是捕盜又病民也。丈田清額，美意也；計額盈者率得褒與，妄益名田以應令，是丈田又病民也。鍰贖
translation_en:
… [give rest and] nourishment to their people, in the Han they praised Emperors Wen and Jing, in the Tang they praised Emperor Taizong, and in the Song they praised Emperors Zhenzong and Renzong. Was this solely because they personally practiced the virtue of frugality? When the ruler's intention lies in nourishing the people, he need not enforce the law to the fullest extent. Laws exist only to bring peace to the people; if a law does not suit the people, it is better to let the law have loopholes than to distress the people on its account. Therefore, in those times they mostly encouraged and employed lenient, mild, simple, and unpretentious officials, while rejecting and keeping at a distance harsh, severe, and overbearing men. Officials are indeed like wet nurses and guardians; if the wet nurses and guardians are not the right people and one does not sincerely seek out the right ones, what is the use of multiplying precautions?

Nowadays, if the authorities in charge fail to uphold the laws exactly as ordered, reprimands and punishments follow immediately. Even when the people cannot bear the burden, the officials still win glorious reputations of dazzling immediate success and then move on to promotion—so who will speak up for the people? Administrative orders originate from the Ministries, the Censorate, the Grand Coordinators, the Regional Inspectors, the Provincial Administrations, and the Circuits, and pass down until they stop at the local authorities. How do the local authorities respond to their superiors? When the upper stream flows swiftly, the lower stream bursts its banks; by the time orders reach the common people, all the harsh and urgent constraints imposed from above are borne entirely by them, and there is nothing they can say. The southeast is a region of wealth and revenue, so administrative orders there are especially numerous and arrive first; vexatious disturbances arise in a hundred ways, and the people never get to dwell in peace or find a secure foothold.

For instance, storing grain to prepare against famine is a fine intention; yet when accounting orders strictly demand that the quota be met, officials arbitrarily impose petty fines to fill it, and thus storing grain harms the people. Catching bandits to bring peace to the people is a fine intention; yet when accounting orders strictly demand that arrests be made, officials track down innocent people and label them as bandits to deceive their superiors, and thus catching bandits also harms the people. Surveying farmland to clear up tax quotas is a fine intention; yet because those who report a surplus in the quota generally receive praise and rewards, officials arbitrarily inflate the registered acreage to comply with the order, and thus surveying farmland also harms the people. As for redemption fines…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
清解矣而餽遺養交日以甚名廉巧奪不
如其明也使者按部每歲議裁節下里會
不沾銖兩民能握算與有司操羸羨乎裁
此盈彼且數倍矣歲漕帑輸誠有程期諸
所留積賦不可少緩時日乎一切朘徵趣
辦以便已事隴穗未登課目已報華楚所
求助歲爲虐如此數年宜其竭也自昔海
波不靖加賦餉兵其後司道有司歲有增
辦數年前建行條鞭法盡舉而入秋糧之
===
額即今歲辦賦視嘉靖初加倍焉譬之貧
家之壤粗銍交加密若魚鱗民不謂至急
