乎而何黠桀也淵魚戒太察獄市以兼容
今之食於官府與供事郵傳者盡從革削
不知此輩能秉耒耜耕乎抑黃馘牖下甘
心不爲不義也數年以來大都政過察而
令必行愚民不能自存姦民無所容納而
怨讟易起有司視司道以緩急司道視撫
按以轉移撫按之臣所寄一方之重者亦
punctuated: 清解矣，而餽遺養交日以甚，名廉巧奪，不如其明也。使者按部，每歲議裁節，下里會不沾銖兩，民能握算與有司操羸羨乎？裁此盈彼，且數倍矣。歲漕帑輸，誠有程期，諸所留積賦，不可少緩時日乎？一切朘徵趣辦以便已事，隴穗未登，課目已報，華楚所加，助歲爲虐。如此數年，宜其竭也。自昔海波不靖，加賦餉兵，其後司道有司，歲有增辦，數年前建行條鞭法，盡舉而入秋糧之額，即今歲辦賦視嘉靖初加倍焉。譬之貧家之壤，粗銍交加，密若魚鱗，民不謂至急乎？而何黠桀也！淵魚戒太察，獄市以兼容。今之食於官府與供事郵傳者，盡從革削，不知此輩能秉耒耜耕乎？抑黃馘牖下，甘心不爲不義也？數年以來，大都政過察而令必行，愚民不能自存，姦民無所容納，而怨讟易起。有司視司道以緩急，司道視撫按以轉移，撫按之臣，所寄一方之重者，亦
translation_en: …are cleared and forwarded, yet gift-giving and cultivating connections grow worse by the day; making a show of integrity while seizing by stealth is worse than doing so openly. When regional inspectors tour their circuits, every year they deliberate on cutting and economizing, yet the lower villages never benefit by a single fraction of an ounce of silver. Can the common people hold the counting rods and vie with local officials over surpluses? Cut here and it swells there, and by severalfold at that. The annual tribute grain and treasury remittances truly have fixed deadlines, but as for the various retained and accumulated taxes, could they not be granted a brief grace period? Instead, everything is harshly exacted and urgently procured to suit the officials' own convenience. Before the ears of grain in the fields have even ripened, the tax quotas are already reported as fulfilled; the application of the whipping rod aids the bad year in wreaking cruelty. After several years of this, it is no wonder the people are exhausted. In the past, when the seas were unpacified, surtaxes were levied to provision the troops. Thereafter, the provincial circuits and local officials added further procurements every year. Several years ago, when the Single Whip Law (Tiaobian fa) was instituted, all of these were swept together and incorporated into the autumn grain quota, so that today's annual tax assessments are double what they were at the beginning of the Jiajing reign (1522–1566). Compare this to the plot of a poor family, where hoe and sickle ply back and forth as densely as fish scales—would the people not call this extreme urgency? What room is left for craftiness or defiance! The proverb warns that fish in the deep dislike overly keen scrutiny, and that prisons and markets require broad tolerance. Nowadays, those who draw their keep from government offices and those who serve at the postal relay stations have all been dismissed or had their stipends cut. Do we know whether such men are able to take up plow and share to farm? Or will they grow sallow and withered [?] beneath their windows, content to commit no wrong? For the past several years, governance has on the whole been overly scrutinizing and orders have been enforced without fail; simple folk cannot sustain themselves, unruly folk have nowhere to be accommodated, and resentment and slander easily arise. The local officials look to the provincial circuits to gauge what is urgent or relaxed, the provincial circuits look to the Grand Coordinators and Regional Inspectors to shift their course, and the Grand Coordinators and Regional Inspectors—ministers to whom the heavy responsibility of an entire region is entrusted—also…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
若不能自必所嚮背其間自有苛細嚴刻
之風仰流承指無翼而飛不由郵置不書
公牘不數日而行乎天下若神符然其所
及處髓骨咸灌玉石罔分天下竟莫能名
其病也即如有荒不報曰懼不樂聞不敢
也宜賑宜蠲懦濡者不請曰恐以爲罪也
言官業已上其狀矣東南去
輦下遐遠諸所不敢聞不敢請者何限一切
以蔽欺苛擾從事何可勝道薛宣所謂政
===
敎煩碎郡縣相迫促以苛爲高故曰民宜
肥而更瘠則此風猶在也伏惟赫然下
明詔令有司知
上意所在一滌向來慘礉繳繞之習以慈祥撫
循其衆吏有寬和知大體者亟爲襃顯以
風天下民知如是即大安耳霍然病已一乜
之效也夫聖人之畏天憂民也景運郅隆
若墜淵焉今既降災矣室家殷富若痌瘝
焉今既枵腹矣海宇寧謐若阽危焉今既
punctuated: 若不能自必所嚮背。其間自有苛細嚴刻之風，仰流承指，無翼而飛，不由郵置，不書公牘，不數日而行乎天下，若神符然。其所及處，髓骨咸灌，玉石罔分，天下竟莫能名其病也。即如有荒不報，曰：「懼不樂聞，不敢也。」宜賑宜蠲，懦濡者不請，曰：「恐以爲罪也。」言官業已上其狀矣。東南去輦下遐遠，諸所不敢聞、不敢請者何限？一切以蔽欺苛擾從事，何可勝道！薛宣所謂「政敎煩碎，郡縣相迫促，以苛爲高」，故曰「民宜肥而更瘠」，則此風猶在也。伏惟赫然下明詔，令有司知上意所在，一滌向來慘礉繳繞之習，以慈祥撫循其衆；吏有寬和知大體者，亟爲襃顯，以風天下。民知如是，即大安耳，霍然病已，一乜之效也。夫聖人之畏天憂民也，景運郅隆，若墜淵焉，今既降災矣；室家殷富，若痌瘝焉，今既枵腹矣；海宇寧謐，若阽危焉，今既
translation_en: …seem unable to decide on their own which direction to take. Amidst this, there naturally arises a climate of pettiness and harsh severity. Looking up to the current and following subtle hints, it flies without wings; without passing through the postal relay stations or being written in official dispatches, within a few days it spreads throughout the empire like a magical talisman. Wherever it reaches, it penetrates to the bone and marrow, making no distinction between jade and stone, and in the end the empire cannot even name its malady. For instance, when there is a famine, it goes unreported, with officials saying: "We fear the court will be displeased to hear of it, so we dare not." Where relief or tax remission is called for, the timid and hesitant fail to request it, saying: "We fear it will be counted as an offense." Speaking officials have already submitted memorials detailing these conditions. The Southeast is far removed from the imperial capital—what limit is there to the things they dare not report and dare not request? Everything is handled through concealment, deception, and harsh harassment, more than can possibly be recounted! What Xue Xuan 薛宣 described as "governance and instruction being琐碎 and burdensome, with commanderies and counties pressing and harrying one another, prizing harshness as a high virtue"—hence his saying that "the people ought to be prosperous and yet grow leaner"—this very trend still persists today. I humbly pray that Your Majesty will majestically send down a clear edict, letting the authorities know where His Majesty's intentions lie, completely washing away the heretofore prevailing habits of cruel severity and entanglement, and comforting the multitude with kindness and benevolence; and that where there are officials who are lenient, harmonious, and cognizant of the greater principles, they be promptly praised and honored so as to inspire the empire. Once the people know it is thus, they will be greatly reassured; the illness will be suddenly cured—the effect of a single dose [? 一乜, for 一匕]. Now, in the sage's reverence for Heaven and concern for the people, even when the great destiny is at the height of prosperity, he acts as if on the brink of plunging into an abyss—and now disasters have already been sent down; even when households are wealthy and abundant, he feels as if they are suffering in sickness and pain—and now they are already hungry and empty-bellied; even when the realm within the seas is peaceful and tranquil, he acts as if teetering on the edge of danger—and now it is already…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
多故矣所以致此人爭言治安無賈生之□
發憤也乃者淅直屢變人人言東南民困
矣及今圖之不爲蚤計矣天下民情多有
似此當事者夫亦孳孳保民是務毋復後
時哉謹對
第五問
袁應春
同考試官教授臧　批〔反覆數千言深中治體宜録之以𢡟予他日事業〕
考試官修撰沈　批〔言選舉考課深識治體不爲竅言而博洽足以發之必偉士也〕
考試官左賛善沈　批〔經生談時務亦多可采是不爲章句之學者用録之以風吉智〕
===
今天下要務有切於官人者乎官人要務
有切於養士課吏者乎趨向之邪正而世
道盛衰民生休戚國家之理亂關焉是胡
可忽焉而莫之察也文具而實亡則文且
滋害狃於故常而安其便則堅不可破樞
punctuated:
多故矣。所以致此，人爭言治安，無賈生之□發憤也。乃者淅直屢變，人人言東南民困矣，及今圖之，不爲蚤計矣。天下民情多有似此，當事者夫亦孳孳保民是務，毋復後時哉！謹對。

The reason it has come to this is that people vie with one another in speaking of peace and order, while there is no one with the [?] and indignation of Master Jia (Jia Yi 賈誼). title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
猶不遽爾也又于正歲會集黨正讀法族
卿讀法歷書其德行道藝而後詔王授之
爵祿繩繩乎爲賔興之重一至於此蓋其
詳哉若乃肆朝之典僅見於六計弊羣吏
而大計誅賞省方黜陟不數焉非略也其
所以養之者其所以察之者也然五品命
契勸於振德不必聯之師儒也六卿率屬
各敬爾官不必歲爲黜汰也是虞周之法
又兼重而不偏也當其時萬邦黎獻共惟
===
帝臣多士思皇咸有疏附得人致治之盛
超軼千古者夫非此物此志歟漢之取士
其目有三曰賢良方正也孝廉也博士弟
子也蓋鄉舉遺意猶有存者唐之三由雖
學舘州縣與天子自詔制各不同而以辭
賦爲重固舉業濫觴之始也若宋之貢舉
制科諸格愈詳而去古愈遠矣漢之察吏
其條有六始於制豪强終於通貨賄也蓋
式序遺法猶有存者唐之四善二十七最
punctuated:
猶不遽爾也。又于正歲會集，黨正讀法，族卿讀法，歷書其德行、道藝，而後詔王授之爵祿。繩繩乎爲賔興之重，一至於此，蓋其詳哉！若乃肆朝之典，僅見於六計弊羣吏，而大計誅賞、省方黜陟不數焉。非略也，其所以養之者，其所以察之者也。然五品命契，勸於振德，不必聯之師儒也；六卿率屬，各敬爾官，不必歲爲黜汰也。是虞、周之法，又兼重而不偏也。當其時，萬邦黎獻共惟帝臣，多士思皇咸有疏附，得人致治之盛，超軼千古者，夫非此物此志歟？

漢之取士，其目有三：曰賢良方正也，孝廉也，博士弟子也，蓋鄉舉遺意猶有存者。唐之三由，雖學舘、州縣與天子自詔，制各不同，而以辭賦爲重，固舉業濫觴之始也。若宋之貢舉、制科，諸格愈詳而去古愈遠矣。漢之察吏，其條有六，始於制豪强，終於通貨賄也，蓋式序遺法猶有存者。唐之四善、二十七最，
translation_en:
…even then it was not done hastily. Moreover, at the start of the year they assembled the people: the District Head (dangzheng) read out the laws, and the Clan Head (zushi [? written 族卿]) read out the laws, successively recording their moral conduct and mastery of the Way and the arts, and only afterward advised the King to confer ranks and emoluments upon them. How continuous and methodical was the gravity attached to recommending men as guests of the state, reaching even to such a degree—truly, how detailed it was! As for the canons of the royal court, they are seen only in the Six Criteria (liuji) for evaluating the host of officials, while the grand evaluations for punishment and reward and the tours of inspection for demotion and promotion were not conducted frequently. This was not out of negligence; rather, the means by which they nurtured them was itself the means by which they scrutinized them. Yet when Xie 契 was commanded to teach the Five Relationships, encouraging the people through the rousing of virtue, there was no need to bind them through instructors and scholars (shiru); and when the Six Ministers (liuqing) led their subordinates, each reverently attending to his office, there was no need for annual demotions and eliminations. Thus the institutions of Yu 虞 (Shun 舜) and Zhou 周 attached weight to both aspects without leaning to one side. At that time, the eminent worthies of the myriad states all served together as ministers of the Sovereign, and the multitude of magnificent gentlemen all had those who drew alienated people close and brought adherents near. That the flourishing of obtaining men and achieving good governance surpassed all antiquity—was it not through these very practices and this very intent?

In the Han 漢 dynasty’s selection of scholars, there were three main categories: the Worthy and Upright (xianliang fangzheng), the Filial and Incorrupt (xiaolian), and the Disciples of the Erudites (boshi dizi); in these, the legacy of local recommendation still survived. Under the Tang 唐 dynasty’s three avenues of entry (sanyou)—namely from the schools and academies, from the prefectures and counties, and by the Son of Heaven’s own special decree—although the regulations for each differed, placing primary weight on lyric and rhapsody (cifu) was indeed the very origin from which examination writing (juye) overflowed. As for the tribute examinations (gongju) and decree examinations (zhike) of the Song 宋 dynasty, the various rules became ever more detailed, yet departed ever further from antiquity. In the Han dynasty’s scrutiny of officials, there were six articles, beginning with curbing powerful bullies and ending with illicit traffic in bribes and goods; in these, the legacy of ordering officials by rule still survived. Under the Tang dynasty’s Four Merits (sishan) and Twenty-Seven Qualifications (ershiqi zui),…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
如德義清謹與獻可替否等類各不同而
以最善勘定九等則分職程能之實也若
宋之審官考課二院權重而耳目益壅矣
我
朝官人之法斟酌虞周損益近代崇以經術
非有玄儒文史之科也拔以科目鄉貢非
由斜封之濫也注以銓選而功罪之考總
之冢宰糾之臺諫非若膠東增户昌邑空
圄之情相溷也以故士修其學吏能其官
雲蒸飈起以應
===
天子之求雖詩書所稱曷讓哉而邇來有大謬
不然者以士言之率三歲而舉舉之者額
非詘也斯豈不稱才乎然大雅之風微晚
禩之習錮婍節脩名曰迂儒也不則指爲
僞學卽所推名士不過襲筌蹄競風露以
舉子業自雄耳吾恐官師之所督非舉業
謂也夫今之弁絲而騏帶者盡他日所使
爲吏治者也而竟若此此得無與塵飯塗
punctuated: 如德義、清謹與獻可替否等類，各不同，而以最善勘定九等，則分職程能之實也。若宋之審官、考課二院，權重而耳目益壅矣。我朝官人之法，斟酌虞、周，損益近代，崇以經術，非有玄、儒、文、史之科也；拔以科目、鄉貢，非由斜封之濫也；注以銓選，而功罪之考，總之冢宰，糾之臺諫，非若膠東增户、昌邑空圄之情相溷也。以故士修其學，吏能其官，雲蒸飈起，以應天子之求，雖《詩》、《書》所稱，曷讓哉！而邇來有大謬不然者。以士言之，率三歲而舉，舉之者額非詘也，斯豈不稱才乎？然大雅之風微，晚禩之習錮，婍節脩名，曰迂儒也，不則指爲僞學。卽所推名士，不過襲筌蹄、競風露，以舉子業自雄耳。吾恐官師之所督，非舉業謂也。夫今之弁絲而騏帶者，盡他日所使爲吏治者也，而竟若此，此得無與塵飯塗
translation_en:
…such categories as virtue and righteousness, purity and circumspection, and proposing what is acceptable while rejecting what is objectionable, each differed, yet using the "best" and the "virtues" to evaluate and fix the nine grades was indeed the substantive practice of apportioning duties and measuring capabilities. As for the Song dynasty's Bureau of Personnel Evaluation (審官院) and Bureau of Merit Ratings (考課院), their authority was heavy, yet the sovereign's ears and eyes were increasingly obstructed.

Our dynasty's method of appointing men to office weighs the models of Yu [Shun] and the Zhou, and adapts the practices of recent eras. It exalts mastery of the classics, having no separate curricula for metaphysics, Confucianism, literature, and history; it selects men through the examination categories and local tributes, free from the abuses of irregular "obliquely sealed" appointments (斜封); it assigns posts through personnel selection, while the evaluation of merits and offenses is overseen as a whole by the Minister of Personnel (冢宰) and impeached by the Censorate and Remonstrance officials (臺諫), unlike those cases where falsified realities—such as inflating household registers in Jiaodong or emptying the prisons in Changyi—were muddled together. For this reason, scholars cultivate their learning and officials prove capable in their offices, rising like clouds and surging like whirlwinds to answer the Son of Heaven's call—even compared to what is praised in the Book of Odes (Shijing) and the Book of Documents (Shujing), how does this fall short?

Yet recently things have gone utterly and perversely awry. To speak of scholars: as a rule they are recommended through the examinations every three years, and the quotas of those selected have not been reduced—can it be said that this does not match the supply of talent? However, the ethos of great refinement has grown faint, and the habits of a degenerate age have become entrenched. Those who cherish integrity and cultivate their reputation are called pedantic Confucians; otherwise, they are denounced as practitioners of "false learning" (偽學). Even those acclaimed as renowned scholars do no more than copy worn-out formulas and vie in ephemeral literary flourishes, priding themselves solely on examination compositions. I fear that what the official instructors are charged to oversee is not meant to be mere examination writing. Now, those today who wear hemp caps andpatterned sashes [as students] are all the very men who will be employed to administer official governance in the future. Yet if they end up like this, is this not akin to [the child's play of] rice made of dust and soup made of mud…

title: 萬曆十年應天府鄉試錄
text:
羹類歟以吏言之率三歲而一考考之者
轂相擊也斯豈皆無良乎然寅緣之俗成
悃愊之致眇焦心殭項曰拙吏也不則中
以蜚語即所稱良吏不過急催科謹期會
惟榮名是競耳吾恐師帥之重任非榮名
謂也夫今之握篆綰綬者盡昔日所訓爲
賢士者也而竟若此此得無與魚珠燕石
類歟□人之情習之既久一旦而更張
之□□□之則又害治玆欲人才復
古□□得其人愚以爲舍責實無
可講養士之實亡也力當挽之以端趨
向之路請取程頤所詳學制稍色潤焉以
孝弟忠信爲表而廣之諸科俾各業其資
之所近師儒月試之曰某良士其善行有
幾其業所精有幾長令時試之復然學大
夫歲試之臺察三歲而大比之又復然其
試也間對經史意見數十條間經國籌時
數事比雜藝一二家苟得於身心而可措
punctuated:
羹類歟？以吏言之，率三歲而一考，考之者轂相擊也，斯豈皆無良乎？然寅緣之俗成，悃愊之致眇，焦心殭項曰拙吏也，不則中以蜚語。即所稱良吏，不過急催科、謹期會，惟榮名是競耳。吾恐師帥之重任，非榮名謂也。夫今之握篆綰綬者，盡昔日所訓爲賢士者也，而竟若此，此得無與魚珠燕石類歟？
□人之情，習之既久，一旦而更張之，□□□之，則又害治。玆欲人才復古，□□得其人，愚以爲舍責實無可講。養士之實亡也，力當挽之，以端趨向之路。請取程頤所詳學制，稍色潤焉，以孝弟忠信爲表，而廣之諸科，俾各業其資之所近。師儒月試之，曰：「某良士，其善行有幾，其業所精有幾。」長令時試之，復然；學大夫歲試之，臺察三歲而大比之，又復然。其試也，間對經史意見數十條，間經國籌時數事，比雜藝一二家，苟得於身心而可措
translation_en:
…mud soup? Speaking of officials, on average they undergo an evaluation once every three years, and those coming to be evaluated are so numerous that their carriage hubs clash together; how could there be no worthy men at all among them? Yet the custom of currying favor and pulling strings has become established, while sincere and unadorned devotion is rare. Those who rack their brains and remain unyielding are called inept officials; otherwise, they are struck down by baseless slander. Even those acclaimed as able officials do no more than press urgently for tax collection and strictly observe deadlines and reporting schedules, competing only for glorious reputations. I fear that the heavy responsibility of acting as teachers and leaders of the people does not mean merely seeking a glorious reputation. Now, those today who grasp the official seal and wear the ribbon of office are all men who in former days were trained to be worthy scholars; yet in the end they are like this. Is this not akin to mistaking fish eyes for pearls or Yan stones for jade?

[?] human nature is such that when people have grown accustomed to something for a long time, if one suddenly alters it [?], yet if one [?] it, that too harms governance. Now, if we wish to restore talent to the level of antiquity and [?] obtain the right men, I foolishly believe that apart from demanding substantive reality, there is nothing worth discussing. When the substance of nurturing scholars is lost, we must forcefully turn the tide in order to rectify the path of their aspirations. I beg that we take the school regulations detailed by Cheng Yi 程頤 and slightly embellish and adapt them, making filial piety, fraternal respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness the outward standard, while broadening the curriculum into various branches so that each student may specialize in what is closest to his natural endowments. The Confucian instructors should examine them monthly, saying: "So-and-so is a worthy scholar; how many good deeds has he performed, and in how many areas of study has he achieved mastery?" When the local magistrates examine them seasonally, it should be done in the same way; when the Education Intendants examine them annually, and when the Censorate inspectors conduct the great triennial comparison, it should again be done in the same way. In these examinations, at times they should respond with several dozen points of their own views on the Classics and Histories, at times address several matters of statecraft and current affairs, or be compared in one or two schools of miscellaneous practical arts. So long as they have genuinely attained it in their own body and mind and can put it into practice…
